sents: lead
The Sandman is a dark fantasy horror comic book series written by Neil Gaiman and published by DC Comics.
lead
Its artists include Sam Kieth, Mike Dringenberg, Jill Thompson, Shawn McManus, Marc Hempel, Bryan Talbot, and Michael Zulli, with lettering by Todd Klein and covers by Dave McKean.
lead
The original series ran for 75 issues from January 1989 to March 1996.
lead
47, it was placed under DC's Vertigo imprint, and following Vertigo's retirement in 2020, reprints have been published under DC's Black Label imprint.
lead
The main character of The Sandman is Dream, also known as Morpheus and other names, who is one of the seven Endless.
lead
The other Endless are Destiny, Death, Desire, Despair, Delirium (formerly Delight), and Destruction (also known as the Prodigal).
lead

The series is famous for Gaiman's trademark use of anthropomorphic personification of various metaphysical entities, while also blending mythology and history in its horror setting within the DC Universe.
lead
The Sandman is a story about how Morpheus, the Lord of Dreams, is captured and subsequently learns that sometimes change is inevitable.
Creation
The Sandman grew out of a proposal by Neil Gaiman to revive DC's 1974–1976 series The Sandman, written by Joe Simon and Michael Fleisher and illustrated by Jack Kirby and Ernie Chua.
Creation

Gaiman had considered including characters from the "Dream Stream" (including the Kirby Sandman, Brute, Glob, and the brothers Cain and Abel) in a scene for the first issue of his 1988 miniseries Black Orchid.
Creation

The first seven issues were inspired and influenced by early DC and EC Comics, and authors like Dennis Wheatley, Clive Barker, Ramsey Campbell, Robert Heinlein, and Alan Moore, but with issue eight he says he finally found his own voice.
Original series
The debut issue of The Sandman went on sale November 29, 1988 and was cover-dated January 1989.
Original series
Gaiman described the early issues as "awkward", since he, as well as Kieth, Dringenberg, and Busch, had never worked on a regular series before.

lead
The series revolves around Gwen Stacy of Earth-65, an alternate universe version of Gwen Stacy that debuted in Edge of Spider-Verse #2 as part of the 2014–2015 Spider-Man storyline "Spider-Verse".
lead
Spider-Gwen explores a universe where Gwen Stacy was bitten by the radioactive spider instead of Peter Parker, leading her to a career as the Spider-Woman of her world.
Publication history
A spider-powered Gwen Stacy was first envisioned by longtime Spider-Man writer Dan Slott for the 2014–15 "Spider-Verse" storyline.
Publication history
In October, Nick Lowe announced at New York Comic Con 2014 that the fan-favorite Spider-Gwen who was introduced in "Spider-Verse" would be getting her own series after much demand.
Publication history
The first volume ended after the fifth issue with the character carrying over into the second volume of Spider-Verse as part of the "Secret Wars" storyline.
Publication history
After the conclusion of that storyline, a second volume by the same creative team began with issue #1 as a part of Marvel's All-New, All-Different Marvel imprint.
Publication history
After 10 issues, the series was relaunched as simply Ghost-Spider, which ended after an additional 10 issues.
Publication history
Under this creative team, stories featured Gwen Stacy traveling back and forth between her home dimension, in which her identity was publicly known, and Earth-616, in which she attends college.
Publication history

In 2022, a new limited series titled Spider-Gwen: Gwen-Verse by Tim Seeley and Jodi Nishijima was published, featuring Stacy traveling through time alongside alternative versions of herself (modeled after other Marvel heroes) to correct a disruption in the timeline.

Captain Stacy—unaware of Spider-Gwen's secret identity—is more than happy to do so.
Volume 0

Upon hearing about this, the Kingpin, one of New York's most prominent crime bosses, decides to ally himself with Spider-Gwen—for reasons unexplained—and apparently has his lawyer Matt Murdock (Daredevil on Earth-616, the main Marvel universe) send the assassin Aleksei Sytsevich to kill Captain Stacy.

Gwen is unsure of how secure her secret identity is as she hides from her father and awaits the recollection of Frank Castle.
Volume 1
Earth 65's Captain America, Samantha Wilson, shows up to capture the Lizards and Spider-Gwen as well.
Volume 1
After a quick chat with Jessica Drew of Earth-616, Gwen and the Mary Janes go on a camping trip where Harry Osborn makes a surprise appearance.

Following the events of the 2016 "Spider-Women" storyline, Gwen is left limited to seven temporary uses of her powers, which she can activate through a device on her wrist.
Volume 2
After having her device repaired by Earth 65's Reed Richards, Gwen suits up and prepares to go after Frank Castle.
Volume 2
Two weeks later, Gwen is approached by Matt Murdock, Earth 65's Kingpin, who she makes a deal with.
Villains
The cause of his blindness is the same as his Earth-616 counterpart.

Agent and the Earth-65 version of Jessica Drew / Spider-Woman that sided with Cindy Moon after she cured him of his radiation poisoning.

modn_amazin_spyder_man_361.title: Carnage (character)

aliases: Spider-Carnage, Carnage Cosmic, Superior Carnage, Red Goblin, The Red Slayer, Goblin Childe, The Crimson Leviathan
powers: All powers of the predecessor's first human host, Spider-Man

sents: lead

Carnage is a supervillain appearing in American comic books published by Marvel Comics, usually as an adversary of Spider-Man and the archenemy of its parent Venom, in particular the Eddie Brock incarnation.
lead

The character made its first full appearance in The Amazing Spider-Man #361 (April 1992), and was created by writer David Michelinie and artist Mark Bagley, although the first published artwork of Carnage was penciled by Chris Marrinan.
lead

Stan Lee would also have some input in the character's name and attributes, pushing for a villain who was darker and more vicious than Venom, due to the latter's scrupulous character development and evolution into an antihero.
lead
Carnage belongs to a race of amorphous parasitic extraterrestrial organisms known as symbiotes, which form a symbiotic bond with their hosts and give them super-human abilities.
lead
Originating as an offspring of Venom, Carnage is much more powerful than its parent symbiote because of the symbiotes' biology, and is in many ways a darker version of him.
lead

Like Venom, Carnage has had multiple hosts over the years, but its most infamous one remains its first – serial killer Cletus Kasady, whose sadistic personality perfectly matches that of the symbiote.
lead

Other notable hosts include Ben Reilly, Karl Malus, and Norman Osborn, as well as Gwen Stacy and Mary Jane Watson in the alternate Ultimate Marvel (Earth-1610) and Spider-Gwen (Earth-65) continuities.
lead
The Carnage symbiote gave birth to its first significant offspring, Toxin, in 2004.
Conception and creation
Carnage was in part only created due to Venom's immense popularity with fans.
Conception and creation
The character was originally meant to be named "Chaos", until a different company came out with a character with the same name.
Conception and creation
Then "Ravage" was considered before Michelinie discovered Ravage 2099 was soon to be released.
Cletus Kasady
Kasady and the symbiote would then be the main antagonist in "Maximum Carnage" and Kasady would continually be the most recurring character to use the Carnage symbiote in many publications.
Superior Carnage (Karl Malus)
Klaw tries to stop him, but due to his weapon being damaged, he fails and realizes that the only way is for Wizard to take back control.
Superior Carnage (Karl Malus)
Klaw tries to get Wizard to control Carnage again but is killed by Carnage and the explosion separates the Symbiote from its host, only to bond with the injured Wizard.
Red Goblin (Norman Osborn)
Following the events of Secret Empire, the Carnage symbiote was stolen from an old S.H.I.E.L.D. storehouse by the then-powerless Norman Osborn.
Arthur Krane
Inspired by what Eddie had done, Carnage formulated a new plan to make a comeback using the power Knull had bequeathed to create a rival Hive with itself as its nexus.
Powers and abilities
Carnage also has the unique ability to warp its appendages into different arms, legs, and even wings.
Powers and abilities
Like Venom, he can make the symbiote look like normal clothing (which he has done on rare occasion), or act as "camouflage" to an extent.
Powers and abilities
In some interpretations, the Carnage symbiote is vampiric, feeding on and thus endangering its victims by only a mere touch.
Powers and abilities
Using these last two abilities, Carnage absorbed the five Iron Rangers, grew to an enormous size, and became blue.
Powers and abilities
Finally, Carnage's powers have always been abnormally enhanced from the maniacal will and insane worldview that Kasady has had from the age of 8 years old.
Powers and abilities
On rare occasions, however, he has deliberately spared individuals to serve as witnesses for others: for instance, Joe Robertson's wife Martha during Savage Rebirth.
Reception
In 2020, CBR.com ranked Carnage 2nd in their "Marvel: Dark Spider-Man Villains, Ranked From Lamest To Coolest" list.
Reception
In 2022, Screen Rant included Carnage in their "10 Spider-Man Villains That Are Smarter Than They Seem" list.
Reception
In 2022, CBR.com ranked Carnage 1st in their "10 Most Violent Spider-Man Villains" list.
Earth-15
On Earth-15, Carnage bonded with Spider-Man and went on to join Weapon X, a counterpart to the Exiles.
Earth-65
On Earth-65, home universe of Spider-Woman, Mary Jane Watson was forcibly bonded with Carnage, drawing power from her secret love-hate and envy of Spider-Woman.
Marvel 2099
In the unified Marvel 2099 reality of Earth-2099, Carnage is a modified version of the Venom symbiote.
MC2
In the MC2 future timeline, Carnage, also known as Specimen 297, bonds with Spider-Girl's friend Moose Mansfield, who wants to use the symbiote to cure his father from cancer.
Television

The first version is a mutated form of the Venom symbiote that appears in a self-titled second season episode and is created by the Green Goblin after injecting Peter Parker with a symbiote sample to turn him into the perfect symbiote.
Film

In Venom: The Last Dance, a symbiote based on the Ultimate Marvel version of Carnage, nicknamed "Lava" by the film's visual effects supervisors, helps Venom and other symbiotes fight against a Xenophage until being devoured by it.
Video games

The Cletus Kasady incarnation of Carnage appears as a boss in The Amazing Spider-Man 2 (1992), Spider-Man and the X-Men: Arcade's Revenge, The Amazing Spider-Man: Lethal Foes, Spider-Man and Venom: Maximum Carnage, and Venom/Spider-Man: Separation Anxiety.
Video games
The Cletus Kasady incarnation of Carnage appears in Spider-Man (2000), voiced by Dee Bradley Baker.
Video games

While helping Doctor Octopus infect New York with symbiotes cloned from itself, the Carnage symbiote separates from Kasady and merges with Doc Ock, turning him into Monster Ock, only to be defeated by Spider-Man.
Video games
The Ultimate Marvel incarnation of the Carnage symbiote appears as a boss in Ultimate Spider-Man (2005).
Video games
The Cletus Kasady incarnation of Carnage appears as a playable character in the PS3, PS4, Xbox 360, Xbox One, and PC versions of Marvel: Ultimate Alliance 2.
Video games
He also appears as a DLC character for the PS3 and Xbox 360 versions.
Video games
The Cletus Kasady incarnation of Carnage appears as the final boss of The Amazing Spider-Man 2 (2014), voiced by David Agranov.
Video games
The Cletus Kasady incarnation of Carnage appears as a playable character in Lego Marvel Super Heroes 2.
Video games
During the game, Green Goblin 2099 uses a shard of the Nexus of All Realities to fuse Venom and Carnage into a new creature he can control that Spider-Man dubs "Carnom".
Miscellaneous
The comedy rock group Green Jellÿ released a song called "Carnage Rules" for their album 333, which focuses on Carnage.
Miscellaneous
During the 2002 Halloween Horror Nights, Universal Orlando's Islands of Adventure featured a haunted maze entitled "Maximum Carnage".

modn_supraman_75.title: The Death of Superman

caption: Cover of Superman, vol. 2, #75 (Jan 1993).
Art by Dan Jurgens and Brett Breeding.
alt: Superman's tattered cape is wrapped around a damaged pole rising from a pile of debris. Two shadowing buildings frame the image in the background and mourners can be seen near them. The sky is purple and cloudy.
tpb3: The Death and Return of Superman Omnibus

sents: lead
"The Death of Superman" is a crossover story event mostly featured in DC Comics' Superman-related publications.
lead
The crossover, which originated from editor Mike Carlin and writers Dan Jurgens, Roger Stern, Louise Simonson, Jerry Ordway, and Karl Kesel, began in December 1992 and lasted until October 1993.
lead
It was published in Superman, Action Comics, The Adventures of Superman, Superman: The Man of Steel, Justice League America, and Green Lantern.
lead
Since its initial publication, "The Death of Superman" has been reprinted in various formats and editions.
lead

Development began after a planned story, in which Clark Kent (Superman) and Lois Lane would be married, was postponed to coincide with a similar storyline in the television series Lois & Clark: The New Adventures of Superman.
lead
While pitching possible replacements, Ordway jokingly suggested that they should kill Superman.
lead
As Superman comic sales had declined in recent years, the writing teams felt the character had been taken for granted and decided to temporarily kill him to emphasize his importance.
lead
They wanted the crossover to surprise readers and show Superman is not invincible.
Background
The character debuted in Action Comics #1 on April 18, 1938, to immediate success, and the following year became the first superhero to headline his own comic book, Superman.
Background
In 1985, DC launched the crossover event Crisis on Infinite Earths, which took place in a variety of comics.
Background
Writer/artist John Byrne re-envisioned Superman in his 1986 limited series, The Man of Steel.
Background
The following year, Byrne relaunched Superman with a new first issue and the original series was renamed The Adventures of Superman.
Background
The relaunch was a major success for DC and The Man of Steel #1 became the bestselling comic book issue of 1986.
Background
Ordway began to write The Adventures of Superman, while Roger Stern, who had recently finished a 12-year stint at rival publisher Marvel Comics, took over Action Comics.
Background
Connecting stories also became harder due to the new, more diverse creative teams, whereas Byrne had managed most of them on his own.
Background
To control consistency in stories, the teams regularly attended a "Superman Summit", which started in 1988.
Background
The summit was a unique method of making the writers work together, focusing their attention to the next year's worth of stories.
Background
Carlin recalled that he had to act like a "babysitter" for the 18 creators during summits, and the teams often compromised.
Background
A new Superman comic was released every week, each selling roughly 150,000 copies an issue—"a fraction" of the numbers bestselling comics like those featuring Spider-Man enjoyed.
Background
According to Carlin, they developed the wedding arc between 1990 and 1991, and planned for it to conclude in The Adventures of Superman #500 (June 1993).
Development
The postponement disappointed the writing teams, as they had to put aside a year's worth of story planning and, according to Simonson, essentially had to come up with something at the last minute.
Development
At the 1991 summit, Ordway again made his joke, but no one laughed.
Development
Bogdanove recalled how the story "almost began to write itself, from the end backwards.
Development
"The Death of Superman" forced DC to cancel a non-canon, four-issue limited series Neil Gaiman and Matt Wagner were working on, as it also featured the character's death.
Development
The initial plan called for Superman to be killed in Superman #75 (January 1993) and resurrected in The Adventures of Superman #500, as both were milestone issues.
Development
Jurgens' design—a massive, muscular humanoid with bones ripping through his skin, inspired by the design style of Image Comics—won.
Development

The four issues showing Superman's fight with Doomsday feature a "countdown" of panels: the first has four per page, the second has three, the third has two, and the last simply comprises splash pages.
Development
The final page of issue #75—a triple-page spread depicting Lane mourning Superman—took considerable time to create.
Development
Ordway recalled the most exciting part for him was exploring what the DC Universe would be like without Superman and had fun writing about other characters' reactions to his death.
Development
DC did not intend for Superman's death to be permanent and the teams kept this a secret; they signed non-disclosure agreements preventing them from revealing the character would return.
Development
Carlin expected fans to know the death would be temporary, and in 2018 said he still could not believe many did not.
Development
The media attention caused Carlin to delay Superman's resurrection beyond The Adventures of Superman #500.
Development

Simonson suggested that each writer create their own Superman, which not only solved the problem of what this new character should be like but also let the creative teams have independence after years of forced collaboration.
Development
Additional replacements, including "Little-Boy Superman" and "Rock-Creature Superman", were created but never used.
Development
The Adventures of Superman #500 was Ordway's last issue on the title, as he wanted to spend time with his family.
Development

Ordway also hoped to use a character from The Sandman, Death, in issue #500 but was unable to do so because of an editorial mandate barring characters from DC's mature comics line appearing in mainstream books like Superman.
Publication
"The Death of Superman" was first alluded to in Simonson's Superman: The Man of Steel #17 (November 1992); after the issue's story, a teaser panel shows Doomsday's fist repeatedly punching a wall.
Publication
This leads to Superman's death in Superman #75, which DC published on November 18, 1992.
Publication
Following the in-comics funeral, all the Superman publications went on hiatus until the release of The Adventures of Superman #500.
Publication
Like Superman #75, collector's editions of The Adventures of Superman #500 came in polybags.
Publication
For Superman #75, DC issued a press kit to stores with a cardboard coffin, stickers, and a poster.
Publication
At the height of the crossover, in May 1993 DC published a special issue, Newstime: The Life and Death of The Man of Steel.
Collected editions
DC published the story in three collected volumes from 1992 to 1993: The Death of Superman, World Without a Superman, and The Return of Superman.
Collected editions
The Death of Superman was released in time for the 1992 Christmas shopping season and, according to comics historian Matthew K.
Collected editions
Reprints of these collections were published in 2003, 1998, and 2004, respectively, while a recolored edition of The Death of Superman was released in 2013.
Collected editions
In September 2007, DC released an omnibus edition of the story, The Death and Return of Superman Omnibus.
Collected editions
A new version of the omnibus edition was published in 2013, while another reissue was released in 2019.
Collected editions
An edition of The Death of Superman containing the DVD/Blu-ray versions of the 2007 film adaptation, Superman: Doomsday, was released in 2015.
Collected editions

DC reissued "The Death of Superman" in four "New Edition" volumes on April 5, 2016: Superman: The Death of Superman; Superman: Funeral for a Friend; Superman: Reign of the Supermen; and Superman: The Return of Superman.
Arcs
"The Death of Superman" is divided into a trilogy of story arcs; the first is known as "Doomsday!", which leads to Superman's death at the hands of Doomsday.
Arcs
The second story arc, "Funeral for a Friend", which focuses on the immediate aftermath of Superman's death, began with The Adventures of Superman #498 (January 1993).
Arcs
The final story arc, "Reign of the Supermen!", began with a prologue in The Adventures of Superman #500 and introduced the Supermen.
Arcs
The title of this arc references Siegel and Shuster's first Superman story, "The Reign of the Superman".
Arcs
"The Death of Superman" concluded in October 1993 with The Adventures of Superman #505, in which Superman returns to Metropolis.
Characters
Olsen is close friends with Superman and designed a watch which emits a high-pitched signal only he can hear.
Characters
As a boy, he witnessed the death of his parents, while Superman later saved him during a construction site accident.
Characters
Eradicator represents Superman's status as "the Last Son of Krypton" and is a visored, energy-powered alien.
Alternate versions
When the real Superman returns, only for him to be killed by Cyborg Superman, Lois kills the latter and continues her role as Earth's "savior".
At release
Mark Potts of The Washington Post speculated the death would not last, but nonetheless expressed interest in what a world without Superman would be like.
At release
Comic book retailers ordered five million copies of Superman #75 in advance and many people who had never read comics bought the issue hoping it would become an expensive collector's item.
At release
Numerous former readers looking for nostalgia also purchased Superman #75.
At release
DC shipped between 2.5 and 3 million copies of the issue on the day of release and it sold out across America.
At release
The issue brought in a total of 30 million during its first day on sale and ultimately sold more than six million copies, making it the bestselling comic book issue of 1992.
At release
Sales from Superman #75 doubled DC's market share in November 1992.
At release
The four bestselling issues of 1993 were The Adventures of Superman #500, Action Comics #687, Superman #78, and Superman: The Man of Steel #22.
At release
Additionally, the first installments of "Reign of the Supermen!" were among the top five bestselling comic books of June 1993.
At release

Valiant Comics timed the release of Bloodshot #1 to the release of #75, and Turok: Dinosaur Hunter #1 to the release of The Adventures of Superman #500 to take advantage of the increased customers and boost sales.
At release
Additionally, those who bought Superman #75 could only sell first printings for cover price a few months after its release.
In later years
While most fans figured the death was only temporary, those who did not felt deceived.
In later years

"Worst Episode Ever" (2001), the eleventh episode of The Simpsons twelfth season, mocks this frustration through a scene in which Nelson Muntz holds the comic The Death of Sad Sack and declares "this better not be another fake-out".
In later years
ComicsAlliance writer Chris Sims believed that most people bought Superman #75 just to see Superman's death, while Weldon speculated its sales were propelled by hopes it would become valuable.
In later years
Sims recalled that when he worked in a comic book store in 2009, some customers were shocked that DC was still publishing Superman comics, as they did not read the story's conclusion.
In later years
Jurgens, for instance, stated he did not anticipate the attention, while Stern believed the sensation was caused only because it was a good story.
In later years
Sims called the crossover DC's greatest success of the 1990s and a definitive Superman story.
In later years
Chad Nevett of Comic Book Resources called the story boring and jumbled, comparing issue #75 to "trading cards that intend[ed] to tell a story than an actual comic story".
Legacy in comics
Despite these similar story attempts, Weldon commented that the industry "was in freefall" and "death/disabling stunts offered only brief sales spikes".
Legacy in comics
Superboy and Steel received ongoing series after the story's conclusion and Steel appears in a self-titled film (1997), portrayed by basketball player and Superman fan Shaquille O'Neal.
Legacy in comics
Eradicator received a limited series, Superboy remained a fixture of the DC Universe, while Cyborg Superman became a recurring enemy of Superman and Green Lantern.
Legacy in comics
In 2011, DC relaunched its entire comics line in an initiative called The New 52, which revamped the DC Universe and erased certain events.
Legacy in comics
The first parts chronicle Superman's actions hours before Doomsday kills him; later parts follow Jimmy Olsen during the confrontation and the aftermath of Superman's death.
Film
In the wake of "The Death of Superman", Warner Bros. acquired the rights to produce Superman films, and hired Jon Peters to write a script for a sequel to Superman IV: The Quest for Peace (1987).
Film

The script, called Superman Reborn, borrowed liberally from "The Death of Superman", including the fight between Superman and Doomsday, but Warner Bros. disliked it due to its similar themes to Batman Forever (1995).
Film
Later rewrites altered the story considerably and the film ultimately never came to fruition.
Film
Warner Bros. released an animated direct-to-video film adaptation, Superman: Doomsday, in 2007.
Film
Superman: Doomsday is loosely based on "The Death of Superman"; to fit within a 75-minute runtime, the story was condensed and greatly altered.
Film
For example, the Justice League is not present and most aspects of "Reign of the Supermen!" were removed.
Film
The DC Extended Universe series of films contains references to "The Death of Superman", beginning with the appearance of Superman's black suit in Man of Steel (2013).
Film
The climax of Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice (2016) draws narrative elements from "Doomsday!".
Film
In Justice League (2017), the black suit reappears as an Easter egg in a deleted scene.
Film
Costume designer Michael Wilkinson explained that director Zack Snyder planned to have Superman wear the suit when he was resurrected in the film, but scrapped the idea in pre-production.
Film
Superman wore the black suit in Snyder's 2021 director's cut of the film, Zack Snyder's Justice League.
Film

A second animated film adaptation was made in two parts: The Death of Superman (2018) and Reign of the Supermen (2019), part of the DC Universe Animated Original Movies line and of DC Animated Movie Universe.
Television

During the 2019-2020 crossover "Crisis on Infinite Earths", a scene set on Earth-75 depicting their Earth's Lois Lane (Elizabeth Tulloch) mourning a dead Superman (Tyler Hoechlin) can be shown on the news after being killed by Earth-38's Lex Luthor (Jon Cryer).
Television
When Lois becomes suspicious of Marcus, she deduces that she is actually John Henry Irons, who on Earth-TUD25 died six years ago in 2015 during a tour in Afghanistan.
Television
The transfer successfully brings Superman back to life, albeit with some limitations on his powers that he eventually overcomes, though his heart is never as strong again.
Television
The third season of My Adventures with Superman is inspired by the "Reign of the Supermen!" storyline.
Video games

Blizzard Entertainment and Sunsoft developed a video game based on the story, The Death and Return of Superman, which was released in 1994 for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System and in 1995 for the Sega Genesis.
Video games

Retrospectively, Nintendo Lifes Dave Cook considered it the game that "finally [gave] Superman the video game justice he deserves in what is undoubtedly one of his most celebrated stories" and IGNs Greg Miller called it one of his favorite games and said it was what inspired him to become a video game journalist.

modn_sagga_1.title: Saga (comics)

title: Saga

by Fiona Staples

sents: lead
Saga is an epic space opera fantasy comic book series written by Brian K.
lead
Vaughan and illustrated by Fiona Staples, published monthly by the American company Image Comics.
lead

The comic has been described in solicitations as "Star Wars meets A Game of Thrones", evocative of both science fiction and fantasy epics such as The Lord of the Rings, as well as classic works like Romeo and Juliet.
lead
It is Vaughan's first creator-owned work to be published through Image Comics, and is the first time he employs narration in his comics writing.
lead
Vaughan has stated that the entire series will span 108 issues, or chapters.
lead
The first chapter of Saga was published on March 14, 2012 to positive reviews and a sold-out first printing.
lead
It was published in trade paperback form in October 2012.
lead

sents: lead

Batman: The Killing Joke is a 1988 DC Comics one-shot graphic novel featuring the characters Batman and the Joker written by Alan Moore, illustrated by Brian Bolland, and originally colored by John Higgins.
lead
The Killing Joke provides another origin story for the Joker, loosely adapted from the 1951 story "The Man Behind the Red Hood!", which was written by Batman co-creator Bill Finger.
lead
The Joker's supposed origin is presented via flashback, while simultaneously depicting his attempt to drive Jim Gordon insane and Batman's desperate attempt to stop him.
lead

Created by Moore, Bolland, and Higgins as their own take on the Joker's source and psychology, the story became famous for its origin of the Joker as a tragic character; a family man and failed comedian who suffered "one bad day" that finally drove him insane.
lead
Moore stated that he attempted to show the similarities and contrasts between Batman and the Joker.
lead
The story's effects on the mainstream Batman continuity also included the shooting and paralysis of Barbara Gordon (a.k.a.
lead
Batgirl), an event that eventually leads her to develop the identity of Oracle, secret data broker for the DC Universe's superhero community and leader of the superhero team Birds of Prey.
lead
Many critics regard the graphic novel as the definitive Joker story and one of the greatest Batman stories ever published.
Background and creation

Artist Brian Bolland conceived the idea for the story after watching the 1928 film The Man Who Laughs, which features a character named Gwynplaine (played by Conrad Veidt) whose rictus grin inspired the visual design of the Joker.
Background and creation
He also recounted that "by the time Alan had finished Watchmen he had fallen out with DC to a certain extent... in the end, he only continued to do Killing Joke as a favor to me".
Background and creation
The 48-page prestige format one-shot comic took a considerable amount of time to produce.
Background and creation

Both Moore and Bolland are well known for their meticulous and time-consuming work; both creators' then-recently finished 12-issue maxiseries titles – Moore's Watchmen and Bolland's Camelot 3000 – had seen delays.
Background and creation
The original editor, Len Wein, left the company, and was replaced by Dennis O'Neil, a "very hands-off sort of guy", with whom Bolland only recalls having one conversation about the book.
Background and creation
The 2008-published 20th anniversary edition of the book featured new colouring by Bolland, restoring his artistic intentions to the palette.
Plot summary
An unnamed man quits his job at a chemical company to become a stand-up comedian, only to fail miserably.
Plot summary
The police inform him that his wife and unborn child have died in a household accident.
Plot summary
In present day, Batman goes to Arkham Asylum to talk with the Joker about ending their years-long feud, only to find that the Joker has escaped.
Plot summary

Batman dodges a series of booby traps while the Joker tries to persuade his nemesis that the world is a "black, awful joke" that is not worth fighting for, and it only takes "one bad day" to drive an ordinary man insane.
Plot summary
Batman chuckles at the joke's punchline, and as the two old foes share a laugh, he grabs the Joker as police arrive.
Themes and analysis
The story is also famous for returning Batman to his darker roots, which changed how the Modern Age of Comics perceived the character.
Themes and analysis

The Killing Joke delves deep into the character's psychology, framing him as being just as insane as the Joker, and postulating that he and the Joker perceive the world according to differing points of view, with the Joker viewing the world as one big joke.
Themes and analysis
Another interpretation, popularized by comic writer Grant Morrison, is that Batman kills the Joker at the end of the story, hence the title "The Killing Joke".
"The King of Comedy"
In 1995, Alan Grant wrote a story entitled "The King of Comedy" which appeared in his series Batman: Shadow of the Bat in two parts (#37 and #38).
"The King of Comedy"

In the story, the Joker kidnaps the audience members who heckled and made fun of him during the stand-up routine he mentions in The Killing Joke, while Batman and a revenge-seeking bounty hunter named Wild Norton try to track him down.
''Oracle Year One: Born of Hope''
In 1996, John Ostrander and Kim Yale wrote a story entitled "Oracle: Year One: Born of Hope" which appeared in The Batman Chronicles #5.
''Oracle Year One: Born of Hope''

The story consists of Barbara recounting the events of The Killing Joke from her perspective, and the immediate aftermath of those events, including her recovery from her injuries and her adoption of the Oracle mantle.
''No Joke''
In 2007, Geoff Johns wrote a companion story to The Killing Joke entitled "No Joke" that appeared in the series Booster Gold.
"Ladies' Night"

The story is set shortly before The Killing Joke and deals with Zatanna and Wonder Woman struggling to come to terms with the impending attack on Barbara after Zatanna has a precognitive dream about it.
"Ladies' Night"

Like "No Joke", the story heavily implies that the heroines cannot alter Barbara's fate, despite their desire to do so, instead giving her a final night on the town before she loses the use of her legs.
The New 52
When DC Comics relaunched its continuity in 2011, many of Batman's stories were erased from history or altered, but the events of The Killing Joke remained intact.
The New 52
In March 2015, DC Comics released 25 Joker-themed variant covers for its various monthly series in celebration of the character's 75th anniversary.
The New 52
Among them was a cover to Batgirl #41 by artist Rafael Albuquerque that took its inspiration from The Killing Joke.
Three Jokers
The 2020 book Batman: Three Jokers features the Joker's pregnant wife, Jeannie, and includes more details about what happened to her.
Live action

Along with The Dark Knight Returns, Tim Burton has mentioned that The Killing Joke influenced his film adaptation of Batman, specifically the origin of the Joker: "I was never a giant comic book fan, but I've always loved the image of Batman and the Joker.
Live action
The reason I've never been a comic book fan — and I think it started when I was a child — is because I could never tell which box I was supposed to read.
Live action
I don't know if it was dyslexia or whatever, but that's why I loved The Killing Joke, because for the first time I could tell which one to read.
Live action
Director Christopher Nolan has mentioned that The Killing Joke influenced the story, themes and Heath Ledger's performance as the Joker in the 2008 film The Dark Knight.
Live action

The Joker's ambiguous, multiple-choice past and depiction as an unreliable narrator who provides various alternate possibilities of his origins, was inspired by the comic, as was the character's line "Madness is like gravity.
Live action
All it takes is a little push", a nod to the Joker's philosophy in The Killing Joke that "All it takes is one bad day to reduce the sanest man alive to lunacy".
Live action

Writer/director Todd Phillips said that the Joker's descent into madness after an unsuccessful career as a stand-up comedian, his past as a struggling lower-class citizen, and his ambiguous past in The Killing Joke served as an inspiration for the narrative and thematic elements of the 2019 feature film Joker.
Animation
Red Hood lures Batman (voiced by Bruce Greenwood) to the chemical factory where the Joker's (voiced by John DiMaggio) accident took place.
Animation
The flashback then shows a fleeing Joker had attempted to escape while trying to claim that he was set up, only to accidentally fall into the chemicals that disfigure him.
Animation
The Batman: The Killing Joke animated film was released on Blu-ray and DVD on August 2, 2016, and also played in select theaters in July.
Animation
The Killing Joke was referenced several times in the interactive film adaptation of Batman: Death in the Family, which serves as a follow-up to Batman: Under the Red Hood.
Animation
The film also reused the pictures the Joker took of Barbara in The Killing Joke animated film.
Animation
Joker reminisces about Batman by retelling Jason the same joke he told Bruce at the end of The Killing Joke before Jason stabs him to death.
Television
In the pilot episode of the 2002 Birds of Prey television series, the pilot episode includes a version of the scene in which the Joker shoots Barbara in the spine, paralyzing her.
Television
The Killing Joke serves as inspiration for the characterization of Joker in The Batman.
Television
In the FOX TV series Gotham (2014–19), story arcs involving the show's "Proto-Jokers", Jerome and Jeremiah Valeska (both played by Cameron Monaghan), are heavily influenced by The Killing Joke.
Television
In Young Justice, Barbara Gordon/Batgirl (voiced by Alyson Stoner) is introduced in Season 2, but is shown to become Oracle in Season 3 during the two-year time skip between seasons.
Television
In Season 4, it is revealed that Barbara was paralyzed after saving the Joker from an assassination attempt by Cassandra Cain.
Video games
In the 2011 video game Batman: Arkham City, the Joker (again voiced by Hamill) recounts his backstory from The Killing Joke to Hugo Strange (voiced by Corey Burton).
Video games
In the 2013 video game Injustice: Gods Among Us, a downloadable content Killing Joke pack includes three skins for the character from the story.
Video games
The 2013 video game prequel Batman: Arkham Origins, makes several references to The Killing Joke.
Video games
The 2015 video game Batman: Arkham Knight depicts the Joker's shooting of Barbara Gordon as one of the hallucinations Batman experiences.
Novel
Novelists Christa Faust and Gary Phillips wrote a novel adaptation of Alan Moore's story, published on September 25, 2018, by Titan Books.
Miscellaneous
One of the two covers of the comic book Darkwing Duck Annual, published in March 2011, was a homage to Brian Bolland's cover of The Killing Joke.
Miscellaneous

A fan-made audio drama adaptation of The Killing Joke was produced by a small group known as Cape Swoosh Productions and released on student radio in 2014 and was commended by Comic Book Resources for its fidelity to the source material.
Reception and legacy
Although a one-shot, the events of The Killing Joke were adopted into ongoing comic book storylines.
Reception and legacy

DC Comics officially retired Batgirl in the one-shot comic Batgirl Special #1 (July 1988), and when Barbara Gordon reappeared in the Suicide Squad series, she was in a wheelchair and became the computer hacker known as the Oracle.
Reception and legacy

Gordon's paralysis was later retconned into a temporary event that lasted only three years in DC Comics' 2011 line-wide title relaunch, The New 52, which saw her restored as the first and only Batgirl.
Reception and legacy
The graphic novel won the Eisner Award for Best Graphic Album and garnered Alan Moore the Best Writer award in 1989.
Reception and legacy

Hilary Goldstein of IGN praised The Killing Joke, calling it "easily the greatest Joker story ever told" and adding that "Moore's rhythmic dialogue and Bolland's organic art create a unique story often mimicked but never matched".
Reception and legacy
IGN declared The Killing Joke the third-greatest Batman graphic novel, after The Dark Knight Returns and Batman: Year One.
Reception and legacy
James Donnelly of Pop Syndicate called The Killing Joke "one of the greatest comics of the 20th century".
Reception and legacy
Van Jensen of ComicMix said: "Each time I read The Killing Joke I'm amazed all over again at how Alan Moore and Brian Bolland teamed to pack such intensity, ferocity and humanity into those pages".
Reception and legacy
Manning additionally called it "one of the most powerful and disturbing stories in the history of Gotham City".
Creators' response
In a 2000 interview, and elsewhere, Moore has been critical of his work: "I don't think it's a very good book.
Creators' response
That was the main point of The Killing Joke".
Creators' response
Bolland says that in 1984, Dick Giordano told him he could do any project for DC he wanted, and Bolland requested to do a Batman/Joker prestige book with Moore as writer.
Creators' response
March 2008 saw the release of the artwork as Bolland intended it: the twentieth anniversary hardcover edition of The Killing Joke is completely recolored by Bolland himself.
Creators' response
The book made The New York Times Best Seller list in May 2009.
Influence on other Joker stories
Critic Mark Vogler wrote that The Killing Joke provided the Joker "with a sympathetic back story as it presented some of the villain's most vile offenses".
Influence on other Joker stories

Moore's rendition of the Joker's origin employs elements of the 1951 story "The Man Behind the Red Hood" (Detective Comics #168), which established the concept of the Joker originally having been a thief known only as the Red Hood.
Feminist interpretations
Author Sharon Packer wrote: "Anyone who feels that feminist critics overreacted to Gordon's accident is advised to consult the source material...
Feminist interpretations
Moore's The Killing Joke is sadistic to the core.
Feminist interpretations
Brown noted The Killing Joke as an example of the "relatively unequal violence female characters are subjected to" in the major DC/Marvel Comics industry.
Coloring
The entire story was recolored by Brian Bolland for the 2008 Deluxe Edition.
Coloring
A printing of the story with Higgins' original colors on gray matte newsprint paper is also available in Absolute Batman: The Killing Joke.
Coloring
In 2023 DC made the Higgins colors available again through the One Bad Day box set, and again in the DC Finest release The Killing Joke and Other Stories.

Gambit is a superhero appearing in American comic books published by Marvel Comics, usually those featuring the X-Men, a group of which Gambit is typically depicted as a member.
lead
The character was created by writer Chris Claremont and artist Jim Lee.
lead
Drawn by artist Mike Collins, Gambit made his first appearances in The Uncanny X-Men Annual #14 (July 1990) and The Uncanny X-Men #266 (August 1990).
lead
Belonging to a subspecies of humans called mutants, Gambit can mentally create, control, and manipulate pure kinetic energy.
lead
He is also knowledgeable and skilled in card throwing, hand-to-hand combat, and the use of a fighting staff.
lead
Gambit is known to charge playing cards and other objects with kinetic energy, using them as explosive projectiles.
lead
Gambit is the superhero persona of Remy LeBeau, a Cajun originally from New Orleans.
lead
He was previously part of the Thieves' Guild before becoming a member of the X-Men.
The character was introduced in-story in The Uncanny X-Men #266 (Aug.
1990), which was written by Chris Claremont and drawn by Mike Collins.
His next in-story appearance was intended to be in The Uncanny X-Men Annual #14 (July 1990), but that book was published three weeks early by mistake, before issue #266 was published.
Because the story in the annual is set after the story in #266, there is some debate about which issue is the "true" first appearance of the character.
Beginning with X-Men #1 in 1991, Gambit was part of the X-Men's Blue Team, along with Cyclops, Wolverine, Beast, Rogue, Psylocke, and Jubilee.
2 #4 (January 1992), Gambit begins to romantically pursue his teammate Rogue.
2 #8 (May 1992), Bishop claims that he has foreknowledge that Gambit will eventually betray the X-Men, but Bishop is eventually proven wrong.
Gambit starred or co-starred in three mini-series during the 1990s.
Gambit volume one (1993) and Gambit volume two (1997) explored the character's mysterious past and his ties to the New Orleans Thieves' Guild.
Both were written by Ghost Rider writer Howard Mackie, and followed up on characters and plot threads introduced in a 1992 crossover in Ghost Rider #26-27 and X-Men #8-9.
A sequel to volume one, Rogue (1994), also prominently featured Gambit.
Wolverine/Gambit: Victims (1995) teamed Wolverine and Gambit on a mystery involving what appears to be a modern-day Jack the Ripper.
In Uncanny X-Men #350 (December 1997) it is revealed that Gambit was complicit in the Mutant Massacre perpetrated by Mister Sinister; the X-Men expel him from the team.
Subsequently, he starred in an ongoing series, X-Men: Gambit, which lasted 25 issues and two annuals, running from December 1998 to February 2001.
When Storm created a splinter group to hunt for Destiny's diaries in the pages of X-Treme X-Men, Gambit joined her in issue #5 (November 2001) and co-starred for the remainder of the series.
Gambit & Bishop: Sons of the Atom (2001) was advertised as a sequel to the character's first miniseries and involves the two X-Men in Stryfe's return.
Gambit starred in a second ongoing series, Astonishing X-Men: Gambit, lasting 12 issues and running from November 2004 to August 2005.
In the X-Men: Messiah Complex storyline (2007-2008), Gambit works together with Mystique to recover a mutant baby that Cable has abducted.
In 2009, Gambit's past was explored in the one-shot X-Men Origins: Gambit.

Marvel Comics announced at the C2E2 convention in August 2012 that Gambit would get a third solo series, Gambit: King of Thieves, that would take him back to his roots as a charismatic, cool, mutant master thief, written by James Asmus and drawn by Clay Mann.

title: Kingdom Come

sents: lead
Kingdom Come is an epic superhero comic book miniseries published in 1996 by DC Comics under their Elseworlds imprint.
lead
It was written by Mark Waid and painted in gouache by Alex Ross, who also developed the concept from an original idea.
lead
The story is set in an alternate future of the DC Universe.
lead
The new generation of heroes have lost their moral compass, becoming as reckless and violent as the villains they once fought.
lead

The previous regime of heroes—the Justice League—returns under dire circumstances, which sets up a battle of the old guard against these uncompromising protectors in a conflict that will define what heroism truly is and determine the future of the planet.
Development
When comic book artist Alex Ross was working on Marvels, published in 1994, he decided to create a similar "grand opus" about characters from DC Comics.
Development

Ross wrote a 40-page handwritten outline of what would become Kingdom Come and pitched the idea to James Robinson as a project similar in scope to Watchmen (1986–1987) and Alan Moore's infamous "lost work" Twilight of the Superheroes.
Plot
While Wonder Woman leads the Justice League to stop the prison riot, Superman confronts Batman and tries to convince him one last time to fight.
Plot
Seeing the third one about to land, Superman plans to stop the last bomb, and reverts Captain Marvel back to Billy Batson.
Plot
Despite Batson's sacrifice, most of the metahumans are still obliterated in the explosion.
Plot
Norman resumes his pastorship, delivering a renewed message of hope for humanity, while the Spectre—inspired by Earth's other champions—resolves to reconnect with the mortal world.
Plot
As the trio leaves the restaurant, only Bruce is amused to catch Norman and Jim Corrigan—the Spectre’s host—bickering over a menu item named after the wrathful spirit.

lead

indy_zapp_comix_1.title: Zap Comix

caption: Cover of Zap Comix #1 (Feb. 1968), art by R. Crumb.
artists: Robert Crumb, Victor Moscoso, S. Clay Wilson, Gilbert Shelton, Spain Rodriguez, Robert Williams, Rick Griffin, Paul Mavrides

sents: lead
Zap Comix is an underground comix series which was originally part of the counterculture of the late 1960s.
lead
While a few small-circulation self-published satirical comic books had been printed prior to this, Zap became the model for the "comix" movement that snowballed after its release.
lead
The title itself published 17 issues over a period of 46 years.
lead
Premiering in early 1968 as a showcase for the work of Robert Crumb, Zap was unlike any comic book that had been seen before.
lead
While working on Zap #1, Crumb saw a Family Dog poster drawn by Rick Griffin which resembled a psychedelic version of a Sunday funnies page.
lead
Its surreal, other-worldly imagery inspired him to think about comics in a new way, as seen in the art style of Zap #1's Abstract Expressionist Ultra Super Modernistic Comics.
lead
When Crumb started planning the next issue, he got in touch with Griffin, asking him to contribute to Zap #2.
lead
Griffin agreed and suggested bringing fellow poster artist Victor Moscoso on board.
Overview
Labeled "Fair Warning: For Adult Intellectuals Only", Zap #1 featured the publishing debut of Robert Crumb's much-bootlegged Keep on Truckin' imagery, an early appearance of unreliable holy man Mr.
Overview
Natural and his neurotic disciple Flakey Foont, and the first of innumerable self-caricatures (in which Crumb calls himself "a raving lunatic", and "one of the world's last great medieval thinkers").
Overview
Gilbert Shelton joined the crew with issue #3, and Robert Williams and "Spain" Rodriguez joined with issue #4.
Overview
Zaps new publisher the Print Mint weathered a lawsuit filed over the Zap #4, released in 1969, which featured among other things, Crumb's depiction of incest in a middle-class family.
Overview
In a related case, however — also brought on by Zap #4 — the U.S.
Overview
Supreme Court ruled in 1973 that local communities could decide their own First Amendment standards with reference to obscenity.
Overview

In the mid-1970s, sale of drug paraphernalia was outlawed in many places, and the distribution network for these comics (and the underground newspapers) dried up, leaving mail order as the only commercial outlet for underground titles.
Overview
Contributor Rick Griffin died in 1991; Paul Mavrides made his debut as a Zap contributor in issue #14 (1998).
Overview
Mavrides was invited to contribute when Crumb announced that he no longer wanted to work on Zap, although Crumb never did actually quit the title.
Publication history
Zap #1 was published in San Francisco in early 1968.
Publication history
Some 3,500 copies were printed by Beat writer Charles Plymell, who arranged with publisher Don Donahue for Zap to be the first title put out under Donahue's Apex Novelties imprint.
Publication history
The contents of the first Zap were not intended to be the debut issue.
Publication history
The tagline of Zap #1, "Zap Comics are Squinky Comics!!" has an interesting origin.
Publication history
Crumb himself credits Gershon Legman's 1949 article "Love and Death" condemning the "horror-squinky" in 1940s comics.
Publication history

In late 1968, shortly before Zap #3 was to be published, Crumb found Xerox copies of the missing pages from the original Zap #1, which (according to fellow Zap contributor Victor Moscoso) successfully captured the linework but not the solid blacks.
Publication history
After being re-inked by Crumb, those strips subsequently appeared as Zap #0.
Publication history
Thus Zap #0 became the third in the series (even though it was drawn before #1 in 1967), and Zap #3 the fourth.
Publication history
1969), Zap moved publishers to the Print Mint, which weathered a lawsuit related to its contents.
Publication history
Zap continued to be published by Print Mint through issue #9 (1978), when the company stopped publishing comics altogether.
Publication history
From issue #10 (1982) onward, Zap was published by Last Gasp (which also published many reprints of earlier issues).
Publication history
Again, there were often long periods between issues: altogether, five issues of Zap were published (by Print Mint and Last Gasp) in the 1970s, three issues in the 1980s, and two issues in the 1990s.
Publication history
Zap #15 came out in 2005, seven years after the previous issue.
Publication history
Issues #13–15 all featured cameos by sex-positive feminist Susie Bright as a character within its pages (or on the cover).
Publication history
A limited edition six-volume hardcover box set containing the complete Zap Comix was published by Fantagraphics in November 2014.
Publication history
Besides including an oral history, portfolio, and previously unseen material, the set also included the never-before published Zap Comix #16 — the final issue in the series.
Publication history
Zap #16 would later be released by Fantagraphics as a stand-alone, 80-page comic in February 2016, with a few changes and additions.
Circulation
The first issue of Zap was sold on the streets of Haight-Ashbury out of a baby stroller pushed by Crumb's wife Dana on the first day.
Circulation
In years to come, the comic's sales would be most closely linked with alternative venues such as head shops.
Circulation

Due to its unusual outside position in the comic distribution industry, a completely accurate count of Zap's circulation cannot be known, but overall sales for the comic's first 16 issues are in the millions.
Jams

From issue #3 forward (with the exception of issue #8), every issue of the title featured a group jam by the "Zap collective", where the cartoonists would pass a story around, each one contributing panels to the overall story (which was usually no more than two pages).
Jams
In 1974, between issues #7 and #8 of Zap Comix, the collective produced Zam (Zap Jam), an entire 36-page comic filled with their jams.

indy_akirra_vol_1.title: Akira (manga)

name: Akira
caption: First volume cover

sents: lead
Akira is a Japanese manga series written and illustrated by Katsuhiro Otomo.
lead
It was serialized biweekly in Kodansha's manga magazine Young Magazine from December 20, 1982, to June 25, 1990, with its 120 chapters collected into six tankōbon volumes.
lead
It was initially published in the United States by Marvel Comics under its Epic imprint, becoming one of the first manga works to be translated in its entirety into English.
lead
It is currently published by Kodansha USA in North America.
lead
Otomo uses conventions of the cyberpunk genre to detail a saga of political turmoil, social isolation, corruption, and power.
lead

Widely regarded as a landmark work in cyberpunk and credited with pioneering the Japanese cyberpunk subgenre, Akira received universal acclaim from readers and critics, with Otomo's artwork, storytelling, characters, and exploration of mature themes and concepts subject to particular praise.
lead
The manga also achieved international commercial success, selling millions of copies worldwide.
lead
Considered a watershed title for the medium, the manga spawned the seminal 1988 anime film adaptation Akira and the greater franchise.
Volume 1: ''Tetsuo''
On December 6, 1982, an apparent nuclear explosion destroys Tokyo and starts World War III.
Volume 1: ''Tetsuo''
By 2019, a new city called Neo-Tokyo has been built on artificial islands in Tokyo Bay.
Volume 2: ''Akira I''
The Doctor decides to try to let Tetsuo harness Akira—the project's test subject that destroyed Tokyo—despite Tetsuo's disturbed personality.
Volume 2: ''Akira I''
Tetsuo enters the secret military base at the Olympic site the following day, killing many soldiers.
Volume 2: ''Akira I''
The Colonel himself tries to use SOL, a laser satellite, to kill Tetsuo and Akira, but only succeeds in severing Tetsuo's right arm.
Volume 6: ''Kaneda''
As his powers continue growing, Tetsuo's body begins involuntarily morphing, and his cybernetic arm is destroyed as his original arm regrows.
Characters
Kaneda (born September 5, 2003), full name Shotaro Kaneda, is the main protagonist of Akira.
Characters
During the events of volume 3, Kaneda is surrounded by the explosion caused by Akira and is transported to a place "beyond this world", according to Lady Miyako.
Characters
Kaneda returns at the end of volume 4, and alongside the Colonel, Joker, Ryu, Kai, Miyako, the Espers and Kei, they take down Tetsuo.
Characters
Kaneda is ranked as #11 on IGN's Top 25 Anime Characters of All Time list.
Characters
Kei (born March 8, 2002), full name unknown, is the secondary protagonist of Akira.
Characters
Kei at first views Kaneda with contempt, finding him arrogant, gluttonous and chauvinistic.
Characters
Tetsuo (born July 29, 2004), full name Tetsuo Shima, is the main antagonist of Akira.
Characters

The Colonel (born November 15, 1977), last name Shikishima, is the head of the secret government project conducting research on psychic test subjects (including the Esper children, Tetsuo, and formerly Akira).
Characters
The Espers, also known as the Numbers, are three children who are test subjects for the secret project.
Characters
23 was shown in the final chapter to have been amongst those "in whom the power awoke" but "were left with crippling handicaps".
Characters
29, 30 and 31 are not mentioned, Nos.
Characters
32, 33, 36, 37, 38 and 40 had died from brain injuries during treatment and Nos.
Characters
34, 35 and 39, who was in the secret base when Akira destroyed Neo-Tokyo, were subsequently listed as missing (they do not appear in the story).
Characters

Akira was the only one of this generation with true power, with the others being evaluated as "harmless" (their considerable powers notwithstanding; they did not, however, represent a destructive threat of Akira's magnitude).
Characters
The three have the bodies of children but chronologically are in their late 30s.
Characters
Kiyoko (born 1979) is an Esper who is confined to a bed at all times due to her lack of strength, which is why her companions Takashi and Masaru are protective of her.
Characters
Takashi (born 1980) is the first Esper to be introduced when he causes Tetsuo's accident in self-defense.
Characters
When he first appears, Akira has not aged in the decades he was kept frozen.
Characters
Akira is essentially an empty shell; his powers have overwritten and destroyed his personality, leaving someone who rarely speaks or reacts, with a constant blank expression on his face.
Characters
Kai (born January 8, 2004) is a loyal, high-ranking member of Kaneda's gang.
Characters
Yamagata (born November 9, 2003) is a member of Kaneda's gang who serves as Kaneda's right-hand-man.
Characters
Nezu (born December 11, 1964) is an opposition parliament member who is also the leader of the terrorist resistance movement against the government.
Characters
Ryu (born May 31, 1992), short for Ryusaku, is a comrade of Kei's in the resistance movement.
Characters
The Doctor (born January 28, 1958), last name Onishi, is the head scientist of the secret psychic research project and also serves as the Colonel's scientific advisor.
Characters
Sakaki only appears in the third volume, in which she is killed by the military.
Characters
Mozu only appears in the third volume, in which she is killed by a reluctant Takashi who psychically turns her attack back on her.
Conception

At his first meeting with the publisher, Otomo proposed for Akira to be a relatively short work of about ten chapters "or something like that," as Otomo said he was "really not" expecting it to be a success.
Conception
Mitsuteru Yokoyama's manga series Tetsujin 28-go (1956–1966) had particular influence on Akira, as Otomo wanted to pay homage to the children's manga.
Conception
The namesake of the series, Akira, is the 28th in a line of psychics that the government has developed—the same number as Tetsujin-28.
Conception

With Akira, Otomo's most ambitious work to date, he wanted to evoke the later Shōwa era, including preparations for the Olympic Games, the country's rapid economic growth, and the student protests of the 1960s.
Development
Otomo began the process for each chapter by fully completing the first page as practice.
Development
Otomo estimated that they would finish the final rough draft at 5 a.m. on Sunday, ink the characters by 7 p.m., and then submit the completed chapter at 8 a.m.
Development
25–28, were taken from Tetsujin 28-go.
Development

The character Chiyoko was originally designed to be an old man, but Otomo felt that was too ordinary and "a little boring" and came up with the idea for an old lady, which then became a large older lady.
Development
The character grew on him as he drew and she ended up with a greater role than he originally planned.
Development
The first 35 chapters used katakana in the font Thick Textbook, chosen by Otomo for its ease of understanding and impact.
Development
After getting tired of this logo and having entered "Chapter 2" a few chapters previously, he used English in Broadway for chapter 36 because he wanted an Art Deco feel.
Development

Otomo was often drawing Art Deco-styled skyscrapers on the title pages at this time, but that stopped when Neo Tokyo is destroyed in the story, at which point the logo changed again and he removed the "H" from his surname.
Development
The fourth logo for Akira, used for chapters 49–71, returned to using katakana and was created by manga artist Hiroshi Hirata as Otomo wanted a Japanese calligraphy-style.
Development
Having come to the "final chapter" of the series, Otomo figured he should change the logo again and went with an English font similar to Impact for the title and his name for chapters 72–120.
Development
During serialization he faced not only schedule deadlines but also page limits and would have to cut content in order to fit said limit.
Development

Otomo painted the cover illustration of the first volume very thick, while its inside cover illustration was influenced by Tetsuji Fukushima's manga Sabaku no Maō and how he used colors like American comics.
Development
Because the first volume had a "hot" red cover, Otomo felt volume two should have a "cool" one.
Development
Because the first three images had followed a pattern of "action-silence-action," the artist figured volume four should continue it and so drew Akira sitting down for the cover.
Development
The cover of volume five was the first to feature an event actually related to the content inside the book.
Themes
The landscapes depicted are ruinous, with old Tokyo represented only by a dark crater.
Themes
The work has no consistent main character, but Kaneda and Tetsuo are featured the most prominently throughout.
Publication
Written and illustrated by Katsuhiro Otomo, Akira was serialized biweekly in Kodansha's Young Magazine from December 20, 1982, to June 25, 1990.
Publication
While working on the Akira anime, Otomo took a lengthy break on the manga, between chapters 87 on April 20, 1987, and 88 on November 21, 1988.
Publication

(The film was released theatrically in Japan in July 1988, and followed by limited theatrical releases in various Western territories from 1989 to 1991.) Even when Young Magazine became a weekly publication in 1989, Otomo and Akira retained a biweekly schedule.
Publication
The 120 chapters and more than 2,000 pages were collected and released in six tankōbon volumes by publisher Kodansha between September 21, 1984, and March 23, 1993.
Publication
A five-volume anime comic version created using scenes from the film adaptation was published between August 29 and December 6, 1988, with newly painted covers by Otomo.
Publication
The colored version created for America by Marvel Comics was published in Japan in 12 volumes between October 7, 1988, and September 20, 1996.
English publication
Japanese manga is largely in black and white, but it was decided that the artwork would be fully colored in the English version of Akira to match most American and European comics.
English publication
At one point, Otomo visited Oliff in Point Arena, California and worked alongside him for several days, but after the first 5 or 6 issues, Oliff said he was given free rein.
English publication
Coloring lasted from 1988 to 1994, being delayed by Otomo's work on Steamboy.
English publication
Akira was the first comic in the world to be colored digitally, using computers.
English publication

Its release in color led to the widespread adoption of computer coloring in comics and Oliff's work on Akira earned him three consecutive Harvey Awards for Best Colorist (1990–1992) and the first Eisner Award for Best Coloring (1992).
English publication

Marvel planned to collect the colorized versions as a 13-volume paperback series, and teamed with Graphitti Designs to release six limited-edition hardcover volumes; however, these ceased in 1993, so the final 3 paperbacks and planned sixth hardcover volume were never published.
English publication
A new edition of Akira was published in six paperback volumes from 2000 to 2002 by Dark Horse Comics in North America and Titan Books in the UK.
English publication
The English-language rights to Akira are currently held by Kodansha USA, who re-released the manga from 2009 to 2011 through Random House.
Sales and awards

The first tankōbon volume, which was released on September 14, 1984, significantly exceeded sales expectations, with its print run increasing from an initial 30,000 copies up to nearly 300,000 copies within two weeks, becoming the number-one best-seller in Japan before eventually selling about 500,000 copies.
Sales and awards
By 1988, Akira had sold approximately 2 million copies in Japan, from the first four tankōbon volumes averaging about 500,000 copies each.
Sales and awards
The manga was published in the United States in 1988, followed by Spain in 1990, France and Italy by 1991, and then Germany, Sweden, South Korea, Taiwan, Indonesia, and Brazil thereafter.
Sales and awards
It was reported by Critique international that by 2000 Akira had sold over 7 million copies worldwide, including at least 2 million in Japan and 5 million overseas via the 38 issues of Epic Comics.
Sales and awards
In 2020, the first volume of Akira became publisher Kodansha's first manga to receive a 100th printing.
Sales and awards

At a price of ¥1000 in Japan and $24.95 overseas, the manga tankōbon volumes grossed estimated revenues of ¥ billion ($ million) in Japan and $ million overseas, for an estimated total of $ million grossed worldwide.
Sales and awards
During its run, the seinen manga magazine where it was first serialized, Weekly Young Magazine, experienced an increase in its weekly circulation, from 1 million in 1986 to 1.5 million in 1990.
Sales and awards
At an average manga magazine price of ¥180 at the time, the 120 issues serializing Akira sold an estimated total of – million copies and grossed an estimated ¥– billion ($– million).
Sales and awards
The 35th anniversary edition won Best Archival Collection/Project-Comic Books again at the 2018 Eisner Awards, in addition to Best Publication Design.
Critical reception
According to Kodansha USA's Naho Yamada, "Akira ignited a new generation of dynamism not only in manga but also in European and American comics.
Critical reception
In his reviews of the first three volumes of Akira, Mark Pellegrini of AIPT Comics strongly praised Otomo's art as "simple, but very lively" and called him a master at drawing architecture.
Critical reception
Austin Price and Lynzee Loveridge both gave it a perfect 5 out of 5 rating.
Related media

While most of the character designs and basic settings were directly adapted from the original manga, the restructured plot of the movie differs considerably from the print version, changing much of the second half of the series.
Related media
A video game, simply titled Akira, based on the animated film was released on December 24, 1988, by Taito for the Famicom console.
Related media
In 1994, a British-made action game was released for the Amiga CD32 and is considered one of the console's worst games.

Related media
On June 9, 1995, Kodansha released Akira Club, a compilation of various materials related to the production of the series.
Related media

Warner Bros. planned to release the film on May 21, 2021, but after Waititi was officially confirmed to both direct and write Thor: Love and Thunder, the film was put on hold and removed from the release slot.
Related media

Legacy
It predates the seminal cyberpunk novel Neuromancer (1984), which was released two years after Akira began serialization in 1982 and was not translated into Japanese until 1985.
Legacy
Akira inspired a wave of Japanese science fiction and cyberpunk manga and anime works, including Ghost in the Shell, Battle Angel Alita, Cowboy Bebop, and Serial Experiments Lain.
Legacy

Legacy

sents: lead
Cerebus (; also Cerebus the Aardvark) is a comic book series, created by Canadian cartoonist Dave Sim, which ran from December 1977 until March 2004.
lead
The title character of the 300-issue series is an anthropomorphic aardvark who takes on a number of roles throughout the series, including barbarian, prime minister, and pope.
lead
The series stands out for its experimentation in form and content, and for the dexterity of its artwork, especially after background artist Gerhard joined with the 65th issue.
lead
As the series progressed, it increasingly became a platform for Sim's controversial beliefs.
lead
The comic began as a parody of sword and sorcery comics, primarily Marvel's version of Conan the Barbarian.
lead
However, it evolved to explore a variety of other topics, including politics, religion, and gender issues.
lead
At a total of 6,000 pages, it progressively became more serious and ambitious than its parodic roots.
lead
Sim announced early on that the series would end with the death of the title character.
Publication history
For the first few years the company's publisher was Deni Loubert, Sim's girlfriend (the two married and divorced during the comic's run).
Publication history
Sim's position as a pioneering self-publisher in comics inspired numerous writer/artists after him, most notably Jeff Smith (Bone), Terry Moore (Strangers in Paradise), and Martin Wagner (Hepcats).
Publication history
In 1979, Sim, who was at the time a frequent marijuana user, began using LSD, taking the drug with such frequency that he was eventually hospitalized.
Publication history
The decision was a financial windfall for Sim, however, grossing over $150,000 in sales .
Publication history
Negotiations regarding DC buying Cerebus took place over the course of 1985 to 1988, offering $100,000 ($ today) and 10% of all licensing and merchandising, which Sim rejected.
Publication history
The series hit a personal sales record with issue #100 which, despite being a normal issue in the middle of a story arc, had a print run of 36,000 copies.
Publication history
In July 1984, Cerebus publisher Aardvark-Vanaheim was threatened with possible legal action by Marvel Comics over a parody of Wolverine in Cerebus.
Publication history
When Sim guest-wrote the 10th issue of Todd McFarlane's comics series Spawn, he donated his entire fee—over $100,000—to the Comic Book Legal Defense Fund.
Publication history
Issue #186 (collected in Reads) contained a lengthy prose section that was attacked by some readers and critics for what they perceived as overt misogyny, and which Sim describes as "anti-feminism".
Publication history
As Sim himself says in an interview with The Comics Journal, "Cerebus #1–200 [is] the completion of the story.
Publication history
Issue #186 was followed by another essay in the back of issue #265 called "Tangent", in which Sim identified a "feminist/homosexualist axis" that opposed traditional and rational societal values.
Publication history
Sim's religious beliefs heavily influenced the last third of Cerebus storyline.

Hellboy is a superpowered paranormal investigator created by writer/artist Mike Mignola and appearing in comic books published by Dark Horse Comics.
lead
The character first appeared in San Diego Comic-Con Comics #2 (August 1993), and has since appeared in various miniseries, one-shots, and intercompany crossovers.
lead
The character has been adapted into four live-action films: Hellboy (2004) and its sequel The Golden Army (2008), a 2019 reboot film, and The Crooked Man (2024).
lead
Hellboy is a well-meaning cambion (or half-demon) whose true name is Anung Un Rama, Urush An Rama ("Destroyer of Worlds, Creator of Worlds").
lead

(His true name is erroneously believed to be "Anung Un Rama" by some, but this is not the case.) Hellboy was summoned from Hell to Earth as a baby by Nazi occultists (spawning his hatred for the Third Reich).
lead

He appeared in the ruins of an old church in the Outer Hebrides in front of a team assembled by the Allied Forces, among them, Professor Trevor Bruttenholm, who formed the United States Bureau for Paranormal Research and Defense (B.P.R.D.).
lead

In time, Hellboy grew to be a large, muscular, red-skinned man with a tail, horns (which he files off, leaving behind circular stumps on his forehead that resemble goggles), cloven hooves, and an oversized right hand made of stone (the "Right Hand of Doom").
lead

As Thorn learns that she and Gran'ma Ben are the only survivors of the Valley's royal family, the Bones are gradually drawn into the events around them, compelling them on a hero's journey to help free the Valley.
