It was the fifth best-selling manga series in the first half of 2023 (period between November 2022 and May 2023), with over 3.5 million copies sold, while volume 105 was the best-selling manga volume from the same period; volume 104 placed nineteenth.
Sales
Volumes 105–107 were among the best-selling manga volumes of 2023.
Sales
Volume 108 was Shueisha's highest first print run manga volume of 2023–2024 (period between April 2023 and March 2024), with 3.2 million copies printed.
Sales
Volume 108 was the best-selling manga volume of 2024, with 1,552,215 copies sold, while volumes 109 and 110 placed third and sixth, respectively.
Sales
Volume 111 was the best-selling manga volume of 2025, with 1,370,154 copies sold, while volumes 112 and 113 placed fourth and seventh, respectively.
Sales
Volume 114 was the best-selling manga volume of the first half of 2026, with 1,006,359 copies sold.
Sales
In 2009, the 56th volume had a print run of 2.85 million, the highest initial print run of any manga by then.
Sales
The 57th volume had a print run of 3 million in 2010, a record that was broken several times by subsequent volumes.
Sales

The 60th volume had a first print run of 3.4 million and was the first book to sell over two million copies in its opening week on Oricon book rankings, and later became the first book to sell over three million copies in Oricon's history.
Sales
In 2012, the 67th volume had an initial print run of 4.05 million, holding the record of the volume with the highest number of copies in the first print.
Sales
One Piece is the only manga that had an initial print of volumes of above 3 million continuously for more than ten years.
Sales
In May 2023, it was reported that each of the 105 volumes, published by then, had sold over 1 million copies.
Sales
Additionally, One Piece is the only work whose volumes have ranked first every year in Oricon's weekly comic chart existence since 2008.
Sales

In the Hot Manga chart, which ranks the top manga of the year, the 113th volume took the number one spot—ranking first in physical retail and seventh in e-book sales—while volumes 115 and 114 placed second and third, respectively.
Sales
In the Book Hot 100, which ranks the top 100 books of the year, the 113th volume reached fourth place, with volumes 115 and 114 ranking eighth and ninth, respectively.
Sales
Finally, in the Hot Shot Books chart—which tracks books experiencing the most significant commercial growth and rising popularity—volumes 115 and 114 placed fourth and sixth, respectively.
Sales
One Piece has also sold well in North America, charting on Publishers Weeklys list of best-selling comics for April/May 2007 and numerous times on The New York Times Manga Best Seller list.
Sales
By August 2022, the manga has sold 2.9 million copies in print in North America (including single volumes and omnibus editions).
Sales
In France, One Piece is very popular and has been the best-selling manga since 2011, with over 31.80 million copies sold by August 2022.
Sales
The first volume had sold more than 1 million copies in France by July 2021.
Sales
The 100th volume had one of the biggest initial prints ever for a manga in the French market, selling 131,270 copies in just three days, the best-selling manga volume in a week in the country.
Sales
In Italy, One Piece had 18 million copies in circulation by April 2021, which represents around 22.5% of the series market outside Japan.
Sales
In September 2021, the limited edition of the ninety-eighth volume ranked first in the best-selling books weekly ranking, marking the first time that a manga reached that achievement.
Critical response
In March 2021, Mobile Suit Gundams creator, Yoshiyuki Tomino, said in his interview that One Piece is the "only manga to trust".
Awards and accolades
It was a finalist for the Tezuka Osamu Cultural Prize three times consecutively from 2000 to 2002, with the highest number of fan nominations in the first two years.
Awards and accolades
In a poll conducted by Oricon in 2008 about "the most moving (touching) manga ever", One Piece ranked first in both male and female categories.
Awards and accolades
In another 2008 poll by Oricon, Japanese teenagers voted it the most interesting manga.
Awards and accolades

In a poll conducted by eBookJapan in 2014 about "manga that children want to read" for "Children's Reading Day" by the Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology, the series also ranked first.
Awards and accolades
The series ranked fourth on the first annual Tsutaya Comic Awards' All-Time Best Section in 2017.
Awards and accolades
In 2021, TV Asahi announced the results of its "Manga General Election" poll in which 150,000 people voted for their "Most Favorite Manga", with One Piece ranking first on the list.
Cultural impact
Luffy was the first statue to be unveiled in front of the Kumamoto Prefectural Government Office on November 30, 2018.
Cultural impact
Jinbe was the last statue, unveiled at Sumiyoshi Kaigan Park on July 23, 2022.
Cultural impact
In 2025, the spider species Damarchus inazuma was named after the One Piece character Inazuma, paralleling the spider's gynandromorphism and color pattern with the character's analogous features.
Cultural impact
In 2026, the beetle genus Luffy and two species (Luffy schillhammeri and Luffy nika) were named after the One Piece protagonist Monkey D.

indy_the_krow_1.title: The Crow
sents: lead
The Crow is a supernatural superhero comic book series created by James O'Barr revolving around the titular character of the same name.
lead
The series, which was originally created by O'Barr as a means of dealing with the death of his fiancée at the hands of a drunk driver, was first published by Caliber Comics in 1989.
lead
It became an underground success and was later adapted into a film of the same name in 1994.
lead
Three film sequels, a television series, and numerous books and comic books (published by numerous companies) have also been subsequently produced.
lead
The Crow has been translated into almost a dozen languages and has sold around 750,000 copies worldwide.
Caliber Press

The Crow first appeared on the back cover of Deadworld #10 (November 1988); James O'Barr provided a back cover to the first comic book Caliber Press published, which contained an advertisement for the upcoming The Crow appearance in Caliber Presents #1.
Caliber Press
The Crow's first in-story appearance was in Caliber Presents #1 (January 1989), in the story "Inertia", which serves as a prelude to the main series.
Caliber Press
The character's first limited series was The Crow #1–4 (February–May 1989).
Caliber Press
In A Caliber Christmas (December 1989), Eric reflects back on happier times with Shelly in the story "Atmosphere".
Caliber Press
In The Crow graphic novel, this story is placed between issues #2 and 3.
Caliber Press
Caliber Presents #15 (September 1990) contained a key preview of The Crow #5, titled "Death" which was left unpublished.
Tundra Publishing
Tundra Publishing later reprinted Caliber's first four issues in two double-sized volumes and printed "Death" (also double-sized) as the third volume.
Kitchen Sink Press
In 1993, Kitchen Sink Press collected The Crow into a graphic novel.
Kitchen Sink Press
A limited hardcover edition was also released by Graphitti Designs.
Kitchen Sink Press
From 1996–98, Kitchen Sink published five mini-series and a one-shot based on The Crow concept with a new avatar in each series.
London Night Studios

Following the Kitchen Sink series, London Night Studios published The Crow/Razor: Kill the Pain in 1998, which saw Eric Draven paired with Everette Hartsoe's bad girl character Razor in five numbered issues (#0–4), plus "Finale" and "The Lost Chapter" in February 1999.
Image Comics
In 1999, Image Comics released a new Crow comic series with yet another take on the Eric Draven story.
Pocket Books
In 2002, Pocket Books re-released the original Crow graphic novel after being out-of-print for several years.
Gallery Books
O'Barr revealed in a 2004 interview that an Author's Edition would contain at least "60 pages of new material that no one has ever seen.
Gallery Books
The Crow: Special Edition was released on July 28, 2011, published by Gallery Books.
IDW Publishing

In July 2012, IDW Publishing published a new five-issue Crow series, The Crow: Death and Rebirth, written by novelist John Shirley (co-writer of the original Crow film) and illustrated by Kevin Colden.
Plot
Eric is shot in the head and is paralyzed, and can only watch as Shelly is savagely beaten, raped, and then shot in the head.
Plot
When not on the hunt, Eric stays in the house he shared with Shelly, spending most of his time there, lost in memories of her.
Characters
Unlike in the film, the crow is not a real bird but a spirit that only Eric sees (and T-Bird, once, at the very end).
Characters
Tin-Tin: The first of T-Bird's gang to be eliminated by Eric.
Characters
Captain Hook: The detective who originally handled Eric and Shelly's case.
Critical reception
The Crow is ranked 37th in IGN's Top 100 Comic Book Heroes.
Critical reception
The best-selling independent black-and-white graphic novel of all time.
Critical reception
Sold over a quarter-million copies worldwide.
Film
In 1994, a film based on the comic, titled The Crow, was released to theaters by Miramax Films.
Film
The film was both a critical and commercial success, earning $50,693,129 total gross during its theatrical release.
Film

A cult following, in part due to the accidental death of its star Brandon Lee on the film's set, has maintained the film's popularity, with a regular staple of movie memorabilia being found at retailers like Hot Topic.
Film
In the late 1990s, a sequel/reboot to The Crow entitled The Crow: 2037 was in the works and would have been set in the future.
Film
Pressman and Malcolm Gray co-producing, scheduled for release in 2024.
Television
A television series, The Crow: Stairway to Heaven (1998), was based on the first film with Mark Dacascos replacing Lee in the role of Eric Draven.
Novels and a story collection
From 1996 to 2001, a number of novels based on the world and thematic concerns of The Crow were published, mostly by Harper.
Novels and a story collection
The Crow: Shattered Lives and Broken Dreams was released by Random House on Halloween; and a year later, in a limited signed and numbered volume, by Donald M.
Video games
The Crow: City of Angels is a 1997 action video game for Sega Saturn, Sony PlayStation and Microsoft Windows.
Music
Fear and Bullets (1994) – an album created through a collaboration between James O'Barr and longtime friend John Bergin as a soundtrack to O'Barr's graphic novel The Crow.
Music
It was originally released in 1994 along with a limited edition hardcover copy of the graphic novel.
Music
The Crow: Original Motion Picture Soundtrack (1994) – showcases the film's music by popular artists.
Music
The Crow: Original Motion Picture Score (1994) – original music written by Graeme Revell for the film The Crow; not to be confused with the soundtrack album, above.
Music

The Crow: City of Angels (1996) – soundtrack to the film of the same name; features a cover of the Fleetwood Mac song "Gold Dust Woman" by Hole, as well as tracks by artists such as White Zombie, Korn, and Iggy Pop.
Music
The Crow: Salvation (2000) – compiled and produced by Jeff Most.
Music
Metalcore band Ice Nine Kills released the song "A Grave Mistake" as part of their 2018 "Silver Scream" album.
Music
The song is directly inspired by the 1994 film.
Card game
It was released in November 1995 but initially had a release date of March 1995.
Card game
The game did not have starter decks, and instead it had a core set with 122 cards that included 10 foils that had artwork from the comic.
Card game
The game was sold in booster packs of 15 cards, but no starter packs were available.
Card game
An expansion titled Crow: City of Angels was announced for an October 1996 release but never materialized.
Card game
Each Personality has an attack and defense value, as well as Virtue, which is equal to the highest value.
Card game
A player wins by killing 25 Virtue worth of an opponent's Personalities.
Card game
Andy Butcher reviewed The Crow for Arcane magazine, rating it a 6 out of 10 overall.
Comics
The X-Files/The Crow: Conspiracy (one-shot, 2014, IDW) story by Denton J.
Novels
The Crow: The Lazarus Heart (Harper Prism, 1998) by Poppy Z.
Short stories
The Crow: Shattered Lives & Broken Dreams (Random House, 1999) ed.

indy_rawr_1.title: Maus

title: Maus
caption: Cover of the first volume of Maus
alt: Cover of the first volume of Maus
creator: Art Spiegelman

sents: lead
Maus, often published as Maus: A Survivor's Tale, is a graphic novel written and illustrated by American cartoonist Art Spiegelman, serialized from 1980 to 1991.
lead
It depicts Spiegelman interviewing his father about his experiences as a Polish Jew and Holocaust survivor.
lead
The work employs postmodern techniques and represents Jews as mice, Germans as cats, and Poles as pigs.
lead
Critics have classified Maus as memoir, biography, history, fiction, autobiography, or a mix of genres.
lead
In 1992, it became the first graphic novel to win a Pulitzer Prize.
lead

In the frame-tale timeline in the narrative present that begins in 1978 in New York City, Spiegelman talks with his father, Vladek, about his Holocaust experiences, gathering material and information for the Maus project he is preparing.
lead
In the narrative past, Spiegelman depicts these experiences, from the years leading up to World War II to his parents' liberation from the Nazi concentration camps.
lead
Much of the story revolves around Spiegelman's troubled relationship with his father and the absence of his mother, who died by suicide when Spiegelman was 20.
Synopsis
Most of the book weaves in and out of two timelines.
Synopsis
In the frame tale of the narrative present, Spiegelman interviews his father, Vladek, in the Rego Park neighborhood of Queens in New York City in 1978–79.
Synopsis
The story Vladek tells unfolds in the narrative past, which begins in the mid-1930s, and continues until the end of the Holocaust in 1945.
Synopsis
In Rego Park in 1958, a young Art Spiegelman is skating with his friends when he falls down and hurts himself, but his friends keep going.
Synopsis
Vladek has remarried a woman named Mala since the suicide of Art's mother Anja in 1968.
Synopsis
Vladek tells of his time in the Polish city of Częstochowa and how he came to marry into Anja's wealthy family in 1937 and move to Sosnowiec to become a manufacturer.
Synopsis
Anja suffers a breakdown due to postpartum depression after giving birth to their first son Richieu, and the couple go to a sanitarium in Nazi-occupied Czechoslovakia for her to recover.
Synopsis
In 1943, the Nazis move the Jews of the Sosnowiec Ghetto in Srodula and march them back to Sosnowiec to work.
Synopsis

Art asks after Anja's diaries, which Vladek tells him were her account of her Holocaust experiences and the only record of what happened to her after her separation from Vladek at Auschwitz and which Vladek says she had wanted Art to read.
Synopsis
The story jumps to 1986 after the first six chapters of Maus have appeared in a collected edition.
Synopsis
Pavel suggests that, as those who perished in the camps can never tell their stories, "maybe it's better not to have any more stories".
Synopsis

As the war progresses and the German front is pushed back, the prisoners are marched from Auschwitz in occupied Poland to Gross-Rosen within the Reich and then to Dachau, where the hardships only increase and Vladek catches typhus.
Synopsis
The final image is of Vladek and Anja's tombstone—Vladek died in 1982, before the book was completed.
Background
Art Spiegelman was born on February 15, 1948, in Sweden to Polish Jews and Holocaust survivors Vladek and Anja Spiegelman.
Background
An aunt poisoned his parents' first son Richieu to avoid capture by the Nazis, four years before Spiegelman's birth.
Background
Spiegelman developed an interest in comics early and began drawing professionally at 16.
Background
The discussions in those fanzines about making the Great American Novel in comics inspired him.
Background
Spiegelman became a key figure in the underground comix movement of the 1970s, both as cartoonist and editor.
Background
In 1972, Justin Green produced the semi-autobiographical comic book Binky Brown Meets the Holy Virgin Mary, which inspired other underground cartoonists to produce more personal and revealing work.
Background
The same year, Green asked Spiegelman to contribute a three-page strip for the first issue of Funny, which Green edited.
Background
Spiegelman wanted to do a strip about racism, and at first considered focusing on African Americans, with cats as Ku Klux Klan members chasing African-American mice.
Background
In 1973, Spiegelman produced a strip for Short Order Comix #1 about his mother's suicide called "Prisoner on the Hell Planet".
Background
He moved back to New York from San Francisco in 1975, which he admitted to his father only in 1977, by which time he had decided to work on a "very long comic book".
Background
He began another series of interviews with his father in 1978, and visited Auschwitz in 1979.
Comics medium
American comic books were big business with a diversity of genres in the 1940s and 1950s, but had reached a low ebb by the late 1970s.
Comics medium
The underground comix movement that had flourished in the late 1960s and early 1970s also seemed moribund.
Comics medium
Most discussion focused on comics as a genre rather than as a medium.
Comics medium
Will Eisner popularized the term with the publication in 1978 of A Contract with God.
Publication history
The first chapter of Maus appeared in December 1980 in the second issue of Raw as a small insert; a new chapter appeared in each issue until the magazine came to an end in 1991.
Publication history
Every chapter but the last appeared in Raw.
Publication history

Spiegelman struggled to find a publisher for a book edition of Maus, but after a rave New York Times review of the serial in August 1986, Pantheon Books published the first six chapters in a volume called Maus: A Survivor's Tale and subtitled My Father Bleeds History.
Publication history

Spiegelman was relieved that the book's publication preceded the theatrical release of the animated film An American Tail by three months, as he believed that the film, produced by Steven Spielberg's Amblin Entertainment, was inspired by Maus and wished to avoid comparisons with it.
Publication history

Spiegelman later came to accept the term, and with Drawn & Quarterly publisher Chris Oliveros successfully lobbied the Book Industry Study Group in the early 2000s to include "graphic novel" as a category in bookstores.
Publication history
Pantheon collected the last five chapters in 1991 in a second volume subtitled And Here My Troubles Began.
Publication history

In 1994 the Voyager Company released The Complete Maus on CD-ROM, a collection which contained the original comics, Vladek's taped transcripts, filmed interviews, sketches, and other background material.
Publication history
In 2011 Pantheon Books published a companion to The Complete Maus entitled MetaMaus, with further background material, including filmed footage of Vladek.
Publication history
Spiegelman dedicated Maus to his brother Richieu and his first daughter Nadja.
Publication history
The epigraph of the first volume is a quote from Adolf Hitler: "The Jews are undoubtedly a race, but they are not human".
International publication
Penguin Books obtained the rights to publish the initial volume in the Commonwealth in 1986.
International publication
In support of the African National Congress's cultural boycott in opposition to apartheid, Spiegelman refused to "compromise with fascism" by allowing publication of his work in South Africa.
International publication
By 2011, Maus had been translated into about 30 languages.
International publication
Poland was the setting for most of the book, and Polish was the language of his parents and his own mother tongue.
International publication
Publishers and commentators refused to deal with the book for fear of protests and boycotts.
International publication
Piotr Bikont, a journalist for Gazeta Wyborcza, set up his own publishing house to publish Maus in Polish in 2001.
International publication
The magazine-sized Japanese translation was the only authorized edition with larger pages.
International publication

A Russian law passed in December 2014 prohibiting the display of Nazi propaganda led to the removal of Maus from Russian bookstores leading up to Victory Day due to the swastika appearing on the book's cover.
International publication
This version of the first volume appeared in 1990 from the publishing house Zmora Bitan.
International publication
Another Israeli publisher put out both volumes, with a new translation by poet Yehuda Vizan that included Vladek's broken language, which Zmora Bitan had refused to do.
Memory
Art tried to keep his father's story chronological, because otherwise he would "never keep it straight".
Guilt

The eighth chapter, made after the publication and unexpected success of the first volume, opens with a guilt-ridden Spiegelman (now in human form, with a strapped-on mouse mask) atop a pile of corpses—the corpses of the six million Jews upon whom Maus success was built.
Language
Vladek's recounting of the Holocaust, first to American soldiers, then to his son, is in English, which became his daily language when he moved to America.
Style and presentation

Art's "Prisoner on the Hell Planet" is also encompassed by the frame, and stands in visual and thematic contrast with the rest of the book as the characters are in human form in a surreal, German Expressionist woodcut style inspired by Lynd Ward.
Style and presentation

Spiegelman blurs the line between the frame and the world, such as when neurotically trying to deal with what Maus is becoming for him, he says to his wife: "In real life you'd never have let me talk this long without interrupting".
Artwork
The story is text-driven, with few wordless panels among its 1,500 black-and-white panels.
Allegory

Spiegelman took advantage of the way Nazi propaganda films depicted Jews as vermin, though he was first struck by the metaphor after attending a presentation where Ken Jacobs showed films of minstrel shows along with early American animated films, abundant with racial caricatures.
Allegory

Spiegelman derived the mouse as symbol for the Jew from Nazi propaganda, emphasized in a quote from a German newspaper in the 1930s that prefaces the second volume: "Mickey Mouse is the most miserable idea ever revealed...
Allegory

Spiegelman's perceptions of the animal metaphor seem to have evolved over the book's making—in the original publication of the first volume, his self-portrait showed a mouse head on a human body, but by the time the second volume arrived, his self-portrait had become that of a man wearing a mouse mask.
Allegory
In Maus, the characters seem to be mice and cats only in their predator/prey relationship.
Influences
Though he acknowledged Eisner's early work as an influence, he denied that Eisner's first graphic novel, A Contract with God (1978), had any impact on Maus.
Influences
Justin Green's Binky Brown Meets the Holy Virgin Mary (1972) inspired Spiegelman to include autobiographical elements in his comics.
Influences
Among the graphic artists who influenced Maus, Spiegelman cited Frans Masereel, who had made early wordless novels in woodcuts such as Passionate Journey (1919).
Reception and legacy
While Spiegelman's work as cartoonist and editor had long been known and respected in the comics community, the media attention after the first volume's publication in 1986 was unexpected.
Reception and legacy
The Museum of Modern Art staged an exhibition on the making of Maus in 1991–92.
Reception and legacy
The Pulitzer committee sidestepped the issue by giving the completed Maus a Special Award in Letters in 1992.
Reception and legacy
The Comics Journal called it the fourth greatest comics work of the 20th century, and Wizard placed it first on their list of 100 Greatest Graphic Novels.
Reception and legacy

Entertainment Weekly listed Maus at seventh place on their list of "The New Classics: Books – The 100 Best Reads from 1983 to 2008", and Time put Maus at seventh place on their list of best non-fiction books from between 1923 and 2005, and fourth on their list of top graphic novels.
Reception and legacy
Early installments of Maus that appeared in Raw inspired the young Chris Ware to "try to do comics that had a 'serious' tone to them".
Reception and legacy
In 2022, the board of trustees for McMinn County Schools in east Tennessee voted unanimously to remove Maus from the curriculum over concerns including profanity, violence, and nudity.
Reception and legacy
On January 30, 2022, it was the No.
Reception and legacy
2 ranks on Amazon at different times during the day, and also appeared as a best seller on Barnes & Noble's top 100 list and Bookshop's index of best-selling books.
Reception and legacy
Student activist group Voters of Tomorrow then announced plans in February 2022 to distribute Maus and other challenged books to students in Texas and Virginia.
Critique
One of the earliest such works was Joshua Brown's 1988 "Of Mice and Memory" from the Oral History Review, which deals with the problems Spiegelman faced in presenting his father's story.
Critique
In 2003, Deborah Geis edited a collection of essays on Maus called Considering Maus: Approaches to Art Spiegelman's "Survivor's Tale" of the Holocaust.
Critique
In the late 1990s, an objector to Mauss depiction of Poles interrupted a presentation by Spiegelman at Montreal's McGill University with persistent abuse and was removed from the auditorium.
Critique

Scholar Paul Buhle asserted: "More than a few readers have described as the most compelling of any depiction, perhaps because only the caricatured quality of comic art is equal to the seeming unreality of an experience beyond all reason".
Parodies
Jesse Reklaw wrote and drew a short version of Michael and Douglas Crichton's novel Dealing: or the Berkeley-to-Boston Forty-Brick Lost-Bag Blues in the style of Maus for the minicomic Low-Jinx #3.
Books

indy_elfquesst_1.title: Elfquest

image: Elfquest 1979 cover art by Wendy Pini.jpg
caption: Elfquest #5, 1979, cover art by Wendy Pini.

sents: lead
Elfquest (or ElfQuest) is a comic book property created by Wendy and Richard Pini in 1978, and still owned by them.
lead
It is a fantasy story about a community of elves and other fictional species who struggle to survive and coexist on a primitive Earth-like planet with two moons.
lead
Several published volumes of prose fiction also share the same setting.
lead
Elfquest was one of the first comic book series to have a planned conclusion.
lead

Over the years Elfquest has been self-published by the Pinis through their own company Warp Graphics, then Marvel Comics, then the Pinis again, more recently DC Comics, and, since 2013, Dark Horse Comics.
lead
All issues of Elfquest published prior to 2014 are available online for free.
Publication history
The first Elfquest story, "Fire and Flight", appeared in February 1978 in the underground comic book Fantasy Quarterly, published by Lansing, Michigan-based IPS (Independent Publishers Syndicate).
Publication history
That company closed after publishing the first issue of Elfquest.
Publication history
The interior was printed on newsprint, and the cover was printed, in a limited color palette, on only slightly heavier, uncoated paper stock.
WaRP Graphics
After borrowing money in order to start WaRP Graphics, the Pinis started publishing with Elfquest #2.
WaRP Graphics
Later, the Pinis' company WaRP Graphics reprinted the story from Fantasy Quarterly as Elfquest #1 with a new front cover and full-color portrait print for the rear cover.
WaRP Graphics
Elfquest was also one of the first comic book series that had a prearranged conclusion.
WaRP Graphics

The original series – generally referred to as "The Original Quest" or "OQ" – ran for 20 magazine-size issues (spanning about seven to eight years in terms of the main storyline), released three times a year.
WaRP Graphics
Color compilations followed, published by the Donning Company under its Starblaze imprint as Books 1-4.
Warp Graphics explosion and implosion

In the 1990s, the Pinis rebranded slightly (WaRP became Warp) and then began to publish multiple titles concurrently, many with overlapping storylines, showcasing the work of new artists and writers on the series.
Warp Graphics explosion and implosion

The (initially) color titles New Blood, Hidden Years, and Shards for the most part carried the main storyline forward from the prehistoric to the medieval period of the World of Two Moons (now named Abode), occasionally featuring non-canonical stories.
Warp Graphics explosion and implosion
A fifth tribe of elves, the WaveDancers, was introduced only to be redacted from continuity.
Warp Graphics explosion and implosion
The first ten issues of Hidden Years were collected in two color volumes, Hidden Years and Rogue's Challenge (Book 9 in the continuity of the second edition of graphic novels).
Warp Graphics explosion and implosion
Selected stories from the first ten issues of New Blood were collected as New Blood and Bedtime stories.
Warp Graphics explosion and implosion
Towards the end of their runs, in the mid-1990s, most of these titles reverted to black and white in North America, though some were published in color in Europe.
Warp Graphics explosion and implosion

In large part as a response to the shrinking direct market in the mid-1990s, continuing storylines were collapsed together into a single 64-page anthology series introduced by the one-shot Metamorphosis.
Warp Graphics explosion and implosion
The new series was simply titled Elfquest (Volume 2), and ran for 33 issues.
Other media
The full-length novel ElfQuest: Journey to Sorrows End, which included both text and several black-and-white illustrated plates, was published in Playboy in 1982, and by Berkley in March 1984.
Marvel
In 1985, the original series was republished by Marvel Comics' Epic imprint in 32 installments.
Marvel

Because of Marvel's 22-page format, these new editions featured additional bridging pages which broke the narrative at different points than in the original Warp comics, which contained 32 pages of story.
Marvel
Marvel's license was only for the original series, which was already completed, so none of the sequels followed suit.
Marvel
Most of the additional material (bridging pages and panels) was incorporated into subsequent print collections and the online edition.
DC Comics
In March 2003, after 25 years of self-publication, the Pinis licensed all publishing and merchandising rights in the series to DC Comics, although the Pinis retained ownership and creative control.
DC Comics

DC's publication of Elfquest material began in July 2003 with The Elfquest 25th Anniversary Special, reprinting the first issue of Elfquest with new computer coloring and lettering by Wendy Pini and two short interviews with the Pinis.
DC Comics
Volume 2 was originally scheduled to appear in fall 2004 but after some delays was finally released in March 2005, 16 months after Volume 1.
DC Comics

Meanwhile, September 2003 saw the publication of Elfquest: Wolfrider Volume 1, beginning a series of bimonthly manga-sized black-and-white reprint collections which arrange the story into chronological order for the first time, beginning around 600 years before the events in the original series.
DC Comics

Wolfrider Volume 2 is followed chronologically by Elfquest: The Grand Quest Volume 1, the first in a series reprinting the original storyline, including the additional art drawn for the Marvel version.
DC Comics
Another book, Elfquest: The Searcher and the Sword, was published in July 2004.
DC Comics
Critical reaction was generally favorable; the major criticism leveled at the book is that it is overpriced for its size (96 pages).
DC Comics
After the four-issue comic series Elfquest: Discovery, published in 2006, no more new stories appeared until the Final Quest, beginning in 2012.
Online release
In March 2008, Warp Graphics began uploading previously published stories to.
Online release
In September 2012, the latest series' Final Quest prologue story began publication at a rate of one page per week at Boing Boing.
Online release
Only about half of the prologue appeared there, deliberately, as a teaser leading to the print and digital publication planned for 2013 by Dark Horse Comics.
Final Quest
In October 2013, Elfquest Special: The Final Quest was published as a one-shot by Dark Horse Comics.
Final Quest
The Final Quest series began publication by Dark Horse Comics, with the first issue released on January 22, 2014.
Final Quest
The final issue, #24, was released on February 28, 2018, exactly 40 years after issue #1 of the Original Quest was first released.
Stargazer's Hunt
In November 2019, a new series debuted from Dark Horse Comics.
Background and setting

The world in which the series takes place – eventually called Abode by its human inhabitants, but originally referred to as the World of Two Moons – superficially resembles Earth, with geography that is marginally similar.
Background and setting

As companions, they brought two of the last surviving animal species from their home, both of which gradually evolved during the journey (and subsequent events) into two more races of sapient near-immortals: the insectoid Preservers and the simian-descended Trolls.
Background and setting

The known tribes include (in order of introduction) the Wolfriders (forest-dwelling hunter-gatherers), Sun Folk (desert-dwelling farmers), Gliders (mountain-dwellers, only a few of whom hunt), Go-backs (formerly hunters, now primarily reindeer herders), and the Wavedancers (sea-dwelling hunter-gatherers).
Background and setting
The main story begins 10,000 years later, with elves and other beings having adapted with great difficulty to their home.
Background and setting
Each tribe of elves has its own set of adaptations and traditions, and most of them are unaware that any of the other tribes even exist.
The Wolfriders
Within their founder group, a female High One named Timmain had been the only member to retain her shape-shifting ability.
The Wolfriders

Desperately inspired by a piece of "magic" lodestone they obtained from the trolls' caves that acts as a crude compass, they make an arduous journey across the wasteland until they encounter an oasis called Sorrow's End, populated by a tribe of sedentary, agrarian elves called the Sun Folk.
The Sun Folk
The love triangle between Cutter, Leetah, and Rayek is the main focus of much of the first part of the story.
The Gliders
Winnowill manipulated Voll so that his plans to leave Blue Mountain again never grew to fruition.
The Gliders
Lord Voll came to believe that the elves were doomed to wither, and that there would never be any children born.
The Gliders
Only the arrival of the Wolfriders with their children and the Preservers could wake him up.
The Gliders
Enraged at the death of their mount, the Gliders attack the Wolfriders and imprison most of the tribe within Blue Mountain.
The Go-Backs
The Go-Backs are the fourth and last Elf tribe encountered during the Original Quest.
The Go-Backs
Originally a migrating tribe, the Go-Backs are named after a sudden desire to "go back" to the Palace of the High Ones.
The Go-Backs
The Palace has a strong pull on all elves once in range, and the Go-Backs were the first to stumble on it since the High Ones were driven away.
The Go-Backs

First appearing to save Cutter and his followers from a war party of trolls in a snow-bound tundra, the Go-Backs are arctic-dwelling elk-herders, bearing about the same resemblance to the Sámi as the Wolfriders do to the Iroquois and the Sun Folk to Mesoamericans (that is to say, mainly in costume).
Adaptations

Besides an unofficial homage in Marvel's X-Men #153 (Kitty Pryde wears an Elfquest T-shirt throughout the issue, and a sprite named "Pini" appears on p.16), Elfquest has been adapted into a range of media.
Adaptations
A scene from Elfquest between Cutter and Leetah in Sun Village was also performed as part of a theater rehearsal in Fantastic Four #242.
Adaptations

While not an adaptation in the strictest sense of the term, Piers Anthony's 13th Xanth novel Isle of View introduces a character named Jenny Elf, a Wolfrider who was magically brought to Xanth from Abode after a tragic accident.
Adaptations
Warp Graphics published the first volume of a graphic novel adaptation of Isle of View entitled Return to Centaur.
Film
In 1982, the Pinis were in talks with Nelvana to produce an animated film based on the story, which was contemplated to open after issue #20's anticipated release in late 1984.
Film
The Pinis signed a development deal with film producer Edward Pressman in 1994, with Jeremiah Chechik planned as the director.
Film
In 2008, Warner Bros. considered to adapt Elfquest saga to the big screen, with Rawson Thurber serving as writer and director.
Film
In 2013 there were rumors of recapping the project on behalf of the producers of a fanmade trailer which appeared a few years prior.
Animated video series
In the early 1990s, an ad for a multi-volume animated adaptation of Elfquest appeared in the comic.
Animated video series
Those who did not eventually received a 50-minute VHS tape from Abby Lou Entertainment, copyrighted from 1992.
Animated video series
Covering the first volume of the book, it consists of color still images taken straight from the comic, some minor animation, and spoken dialogue.
Web trailer
The short premiered at the Screen Actors Guild in April 2011 and the cast featured Taryn Southern, Casey McKinnon, Jessica Lee Rose, and more.
Role-playing games

A licensed tabletop Elfquest role playing game was produced by Chaosium in 1984, utilizing the Basic Role-Playing system which had first appeared in the game RuneQuest and some original illustrations by Wendy Pini, including the character sheets.
Toys
A proposed second series that would have included Skywise, among others, never reached production.
Board games
In 1986, Mayfair Games released ElfQuest, a competitive game where players lay tiles to build the board as the game proceeds.
Board games

In 2015, Cheeky Dingo games released the ElfQuest Adventure Game, a cooperative board game, where the players take four elven characters on a campaign of adventures based on stories from the comic books.
Music
In 1987, Off Centaur Publications released A Wolfrider's Reflections: Songs of Elfquest, a collection of filk songs.
Music
In 2013, several unreleased Elfquest songs by Julia Ecklar were also included on her solo album, Horsetamer.
Starfire

One particular anecdote was the creation of a mission insignia for one of the experiments taken aloft by Space Shuttle Columbia with mission STS-87, which was dubbed 'Enclosed Laminar Flames', abbreviated to ELF, in 1997.
Starfire

The result is a circular insignia depicting the experiment, holding the names of the primary contributors (including the University of Iowa), set against a dark blue, star-spangled background and a unique elven character, wearing a green-and-black suit with star motifs accompanying the experiment.
Starfire
The character, dubbed "Starfire", became a first in space – no comic book-style character had been created in connection with a spaceflight mission, let alone actually traveled to space.
ElfQuest: The Audio Movie
In 2021, the Pinis began to develop an audio movie production via live stream focusing on the first five issues of the original comic book series.
ElfQuest: The Audio Movie
Two crowdfunding pledge campaigns, one with TFN and the other through Kickstarter, were both successful, raising over $300,000.
Cancelled adult animated series
In 2024, Fox Entertainment and Bento Box Entertainment developed a pilot script commitment for a one-hour adult animated series based on the comics.
Cancelled adult animated series
On April 17, 2026, it was reported that the show will not move forward at Fox and plans had been cancelled.

title: Love and Rockets
caption: Cover illustration by Gilbert Hernández for Love and Rockets #16, depicting two of his major Palomar characters, Heraclio and Carmen.

sents: lead
Love and Rockets (often abbreviated L&R) is a long-running comic book series by the Hernández brothers: Gilbert, Jaime, and Mario.
lead
The series is published by Fantagraphics.
lead
It was one of the first comic books in the alternative comics movement of the 1980s.
lead
The Hernández brothers produce stories in the series independently of each other.
lead
Gilbert and Jaime produce the majority of the material, and tend to focus on particular casts of characters and settings.
lead
Those of Gilbert usually focus on a cast of characters in the fictional Central American village of Palomar; the stories often feature magic realist elements.
lead
The Locas stories of Jaime center on a social group in Los Angeles, particularly the Latina friends and sometime-lovers Maggie and Hopey.
Overview
In the late 1960s, the brothers got into the underground comix movement through discovering a copy of Robert Crumb's Zap Comix.
Overview
The Hernández brothers self-published the first issue of Love and Rockets in 1981.
Overview
It was one of the first comic books in the alternative comics movement of the 1980s.
Overview
The magazine temporarily ceased publication in 1996 after the release of issue #50.
Overview
However, after several publications featuring characters from the series, in 2001 the brothers revived the series as Love and Rockets Volume 2, and have continued it since.
Overview
Love and Rockets contains several ongoing serial narratives, the most prominent being Gilbert's Palomar stories and Jaime's Locas stories.
Overview
Originally a young "prosolar mechanic", the early stories contain rocket ships and dinosaurs, before starting to include fewer adventure tales and more slice-of-life.
Overview
Since her first appearance in the early 1980s, Maggie has aged alongside her author, going from a teen in the local punk scene through to middle age via a series of relationships and jobs.
Overview
Huerta is inspired by the Hernándezes' home town of Oxnard.
Jaime's ''Locas''
Margarita Luisa "Maggie" Chascarrillo: called "Perla" by her family; best friend (and occasional girlfriend) of Hopey; otherwise dates men, most prominently Ray Dominguez.
Jaime's ''Locas''
Rand Race: handsome, world-famous mechanic who hires Maggie and takes her on adventures, oblivious to her crush on him because of his infatuation with former girlfriend Penny Century.
Gilbert's ''Palomar''
Pipo, Gato, Sergio: beautiful, vain, successful Pipo; her angry but devoted (ex-)husband Gato, and her son (by Manuel) Sergio, a world-famous soccer star.
Gilbert's ''Palomar''
Manuel and Soledad: friends/lovers/rivals, stars of the first Palomar story "Heartbreak Soup"
Jaime
Home School – using Peanuts and Dennis the Menace inspired artwork, Jaime tells the story of toddler Maggie and slightly-older Isabel becoming friends under the shadow of fighting parents.
Gilbert
Heartbreak Soup – first Palomar story.
Gilbert

It details her broken family, her young marriage to first husband Pedro, his criminal connections and her own drug habits, reuniting with her cousin Ofelia, giving birth to her first daughter, fleeing military conflicts, and her ending up on the outskirts of Palomar.
Volume I
The brothers Gilbert, Jaime, and Mario Hernandez self-published the first issue of Love and Rockets in 1981.
Volume I
In 1982, Fantagraphics Books republished this issue with a color cover.
Volume I
The first volume ended with the 50th issue in 1996.
Volume II
After the end of the first series, the two brothers began working on separate titles that carried on many of the stories in the original Love and Rockets.
Volume II
Sales for these were lower, so in 2001 they began to release a second series under that name.
Volume II
The second volume ran for twenty issues from 2001 to 2007 in standard US comic book size.
Volume IV
In 2016, Fantagraphics began releasing Volume IV of Love and Rockets, returning to its original, magazine-sized format.

Reception
Writing for The Guardian in 2016, David Barnett called Love and Rockets "one of the most original and influential comic projects ever".
Reception
Rolling Stone called it the best non-superhero comic of all time in a list published in 2019.
Reception
KCET broadcast a documentary in 2022 on the comic as part of its Artbound series titled Love and Rockets: The Great American Comic Book.
Reception

Miranda said in the Los Angeles Times in 2023 that the Hernández brothers' works "changed U.S. comics, infusing the form with elements of Latin American folklore and Chicano life" and that "many of the stories feel as fresh and as strange as they did in 1982".
Reception
In 2008, Maggie and Hopey were ranked #95 on Wizard's 200 Greatest Comic Book Characters of all time.

indy_usagi_yojimbro_1.title: Usagi Yojimbo

caption: Usagi Yojimbo, Book 1: The Ronin

sents: lead
Usagi Yojimbo is a comic book series written and illustrated by Stan Sakai.
lead
It is set primarily at the beginning of the Edo period of Japanese history and features anthropomorphic animals in place of humans.
lead
The main character is a rabbit rōnin, Miyamoto Usagi, whom Sakai based partially on the famous swordsman Miyamoto Musashi.
lead
Usagi wanders the land on a musha shugyō (a warrior's pilgrimage), occasionally selling his services as a bodyguard.
lead

Usagi Yojimbo is heavily influenced by Japanese cinema; it has included references to the work of Akira Kurosawa (the title of the series is derived from Kurosawa's 1961 film Yojimbo), as well as to icons of Japanese pop culture, such as Lone Wolf and Cub, Zatoichi, and Godzilla.
lead
The series is also partially influenced by Groo the Wanderer by Sergio Aragonés (Sakai is the letterer for that series), but the overall tone of Usagi Yojimbo is more serious and reflective.
lead
The series follows the standard traditional Japanese naming-convention for all featured characters: their family names come before their given names.
lead
The books are primarily episodic but occasionally featured underlying interconnected plots that form long extended storylines, though there are some novel-length narratives.
Publishing history
Sakai originally planned for Usagi and other characters to be human in stories explicitly modeled after the life of Miyamoto Musashi.
Publishing history
Usagi was first conceived as a supporting character in The Adventures of Nilson Groundthumper and Hermy, a brief series that predates Usagi Yojimbo.
Publishing history

Sakai expanded on the idea of a rabbit samurai and his world took on an anthropomorphized cartoon nature, creating a fantasy setting which suited his dramatic needs with a unique look he thought could attract readers.
Publishing history
Usagi first appeared in the anthology Albedo Anthropomorphics in 1984, and later in the Fantagraphics Books anthropomorphic anthology Critters, before appearing in his own series in 1987.
Publishing history
The first publisher was Fantagraphics (volume one; 38 regular issues, plus one Summer Special and three Color Specials).
Publishing history

The third was Dark Horse Comics (volume three, 172 regular issues and two Color Specials), which also published the Senso miniseries (2015), The Art of Usagi Yojimbo: 20th Anniversary Edition (2004), and Usagi Yojimbo: 35 Years of Covers (2018), as well as republishing the Fantagraphics and Mirage series.
Publishing history
The fourth is IDW Publishing, (volume four, 31 issues), which also republished select Fantagraphics story portions as Usagi Yojimbo Color Classics.
Publishing history
Usagi returned to Dark Horse in September 2023, collaborating with Dogu Limited.
Publishing history

Another publisher, Radio Comix, published two issues of The Art of Usagi Yojimbo (1997–1998) which contained a selection of unpublished drawings, convention sketches, and other miscellaneous Usagi Yojimbo artwork (including an original short story in the first issue).
Publishing history

Sakai has experimented with formats for Usagi Yojimbo, such as when he published the color story "Green Persimmon" first as twelve separate 2-page chapters serialized in Diamond Comic Distributor's monthly catalog Previews.
Publishing history
In the 1987 series, "Usagi Yojimbo" is incorrectly used as his actual name, but in the 2003 series, where he appeared far more frequently, he was referred to correctly as Miyamoto Usagi.
Publishing history
Usagi's first appearance in the 2012 series was the fifth-season episode, "Yojimbo", which was written by Sakai.
Publishing history
In addition, Sakai created a limited spin off series called Space Usagi, who first appeared in Amazing Heroes 187.
Publishing history
A one-shot crossover between the contemporary Usagi Yojimbo (Volume 4) series and Space Usagi, titled Space Usagi: Yokai Hunter, was released on October 11, 2023.
Publishing history
In May 2015, Sakai returned to Usagi Yojimbo with the release of the 145th issue.
Publishing history
On February 22, 2019, The New York Times reported that IDW Publishing would present a new monthly Usagi Yojimbo series, in color (provided by Tom Luth for the first time).
Publishing history
IDW published volume 4 of the series up until issue 31, published in 2022.
Publishing history
The series was relaunched at Dark Horse with Usagi Yojimbo: Ice and Snow #1, the first in a five issue mini-series.
Publishing history
In 2026, a new spin-off series, Usagi Yojimbo: Kaitō '84 was launched.
Television
Usagi first appeared in episodes 32 and 34 in the third season of the 1987 Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles animated series.
Television
He next appeared in episodes 23–26 in the second season of the 2003 Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles animated series for an interdimensional tournament against the Turtles (along with Gen).
Television

He and Gen showed up again in episodes 1 and 22–23 of season 3 for a Christmas party and a continuation of the second-season storyline (which prominently featured his world and characters), respectively.
Television
Usagi again appeared in episode 13 of season 4 ("Samurai Tourist") for a confrontation with Leonardo, although the focus was mainly on Gen.
Television
Usagi and Gen also attended the wedding of April O'Neil and Casey Jones in episode 13 of season 7 (Back to the Sewer) titled "Wedding Bells and Bytes".
Television
In September 2016, an appearance of Usagi was also announced for the 2012 CGI series of Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles.
Television
On February 8, 2018, it was announced that a CGI adaptation of the comics is in the works from Gaumont Animation.
Television
On July 15, 2020, Gaumont announced that the series would be released worldwide exclusively on Netflix under the title Samurai Rabbit: The Usagi Chronicles, in partnership with Netflix Animation.
Television
The show premiered on April 28, 2022 and concluded on September 1.
Video games
A Samurai Warrior: The Battles of Usagi Yojimbo video game was released for the Commodore 64, ZX Spectrum and Amstrad CPC in 1988 by Firebird.
Video games
Usagi appears as a playable character in the Dimension Shellshock downloadable content for Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Shredder's Revenge, released on August 31, 2023.
