title: Asterix the Gaul
caption: Cover of the English edition

sents: lead
Asterix the Gaul is a French comic story, written by René Goscinny and illustrated by Albert Uderzo.
lead
First published by Dargaud as a serial for Pilote magazine in October 1959, it was later released as a comic album in 1961.
lead

The story focuses on a Gaul named Asterix, whose village resists Roman rule, as he attempts to rescue his village's druid from a Roman garrison when its commander seeks to secure the secret of the village's superhuman strength.
lead

The story proved hugely popular with French readers, leading to Goscinny and Uderzo writing further stories that would go on to form the Asterix comic strip series, with international versions of the comic helping to broaden its appeal outside of France.
lead

Dargaud later developed an animated adaptation of the comic for theatrical release in 1967 with its own production company, though Goscinny and Uderzo disapproved of the poor animation quality; they later blocked a sequel based on their next story.
lead
Alongside the film, an audiobook adaptation was created by EMI Records.
lead

In 1999 Asterix the Gaul was voted as the 23rd greatest book of the 20th century, in a poll conducted across France by French retailer Fnac and the Paris newspaper Le Monde for Le Monde 100 Books of the Century.
Plot
Determined to uncover their secret, Centurion Crismus Bonus, commander of the camp of Compendium, sends a spy into the village.
Plot
After securing the ingredients he needs, Getafix tricks Crismus Bonus that he needs strawberries, only for him and Asterix to consume them all once the Romans find some.
Characters
The character's design was oddly altered a few pages after they first appear in the novel.
Publishing history
The story was first published as a serial in Pilote magazine, a Franco-Belgian comics magazine founded by Goscinny and a few other comic artists.
Publishing history
The first page appeared in the promotional issue #0, distributed on 1 June 1959, and the story was serially published in the magazine from issue #1 (29 October 1959) until issue #38 (14 July 1960).
Publishing history
A small head of Asterix first appeared on the cover of #9 (24 December 1959), and a full Asterix cover was used on #21 (17 March 1960).
Publishing history
The next story, Asterix and the Golden Sickle, started in issue #42 (11 August 1960).
Publishing history
Asterix le Gaulois was published in July 1961 by Dargaud in the so-called "Pilote collection" with a print of 6000 copies.
Publishing history
A Dutch translation followed in 1966, and other languages followed soon after.
Publishing history
The English translation by Anthea Bell and Derek Hockridge was first published in 1969 by Brockhampton Press.
Publishing history
The plate for page 35 was redrawn by Albert Uderzo's brother Marcel in 1970 because the original was lost.
Publishing history
The 2004 release from Orion Books uses the redone illustrations from the French editions.
Publishing history
An audiobook of Asterix the Gaul adapted by Anthea Bell and narrated by Willie Rushton was released on EMI Records Listen for Pleasure label in 1990.
Publishing history
On 29 October 2009, Google prominently featured an integration of Asterix and Obelix in its mast head, celebrating the 50th anniversary of the first publication.
Film adaptation
In 1967, Dargaud released an animated adaptation of the novel, under the same name, for theatrical release - though originally, the company planned for it to air on French television.
Film adaptation

Neither approved of the quality of the animation by the team Dargaud employed, and later blocked the company from making a planned adaptation of Asterix and the Golden Sickle, only allowing for further adaptations on the grounds that they had involvement in future animated films for Dargaud.

indy_explorers_on_the_moon.title: Explorers on the Moon

title: Explorers on the Moon
foreigntitle: On a marché sur la Lune
image: The Adventures of Tintin - 17 - Explorers on the Moon.jpg
alt: Wearing space suits, Tintin, Snowy, and Haddock are exploring the surface of the moon, with their rocket ship in the background.
caption: Cover of the English edition
creator: Hergé

sents: lead
Explorers on the Moon (; literally: We walked on the Moon) is the seventeenth volume of The Adventures of Tintin, the comics series by Belgian cartoonist Hergé.
lead
The story was serialised weekly in Belgium's Tintin magazine from October 1952 to December 1953 before being published in a collected volume by Casterman in 1954.
lead

Completing a story arc begun in the preceding volume, Destination Moon (1953), the narrative tells of the young reporter Tintin, his dog Snowy, and friends Captain Haddock, Professor Calculus, and Thomson and Thompson who are aboard humanity's first crewed rocket mission to the Moon.
lead
Hergé continued The Adventures of Tintin with The Calculus Affair, while the series itself became a defining part of the Franco-Belgian comics tradition.
lead

The story was adapted for the 1957 Belvision animated series Hergé's Adventures of Tintin, the 1989 computer game Tintin on the Moon, the 1991 Ellipse/Nelvana animated series The Adventures of Tintin, and the 1992-3 BBC Radio 5 dramatisation of the Adventures.
Synopsis

Soon after takeoff they discover that the detectives Thomson and Thompson have accidentally stowed away on board, thinking the launch was set for 1:34 P.M., and not A.M., putting a strain on the oxygen supply.
Synopsis
The rocket lands in the Hipparchus Crater, with Tintin being the first human to step on the Moon.
Synopsis
As a first-aider, Tintin finally places the bandages around Snowy's injured leg to heal completely.
Background
Hergé first devised the idea of sending Tintin on a mission to the Moon while he was working on Prisoners of the Sun (1949).
Background
Jacobs, who had recently had success with his own science fiction comic The Secret of the Swordfish (1950–53).
Background

He decided that it would be a two-volume story arc, as had proved successful with his earlier arcs, Cigars of the Pharaoh (1934) and The Blue Lotus (1936), The Secret of the Unicorn (1943) and Red Rackham's Treasure (1944), and The Seven Crystal Balls (1948) and Prisoners of the Sun.
Background
Seeking advice on the story, Hergé consulted his friend Bernard Heuvelmans, who had authored the non-fiction book L'Homme parmi les étoiles ("Man Among the Stars") (1944).
Background
In autumn 1947, Heuvelmans and Jacques Van Melkebeke developed a script for the story, which they gave to Hergé.
Background
In early 1948, Hergé produced two black-and-white pages of this version of the story before abandoning it.
Background

Hergé retained some elements of this original script in his finished version, namely the scenes in which Captain Haddock drinks whiskey in a gravity-free environment and that in which he goes for a space walk and nearly becomes a satellite of Adonis, which appear on pages 5 and 8 of Explorers on the Moon.
Background

Nevertheless, Heuvelmans thought his influence on the story to be more significant, stating that "in going through the two books we [he and Van Melkebeke] really had the impression that it was what we had originally done at the beginning.
Background
A further work that he used was L'Astronautique (1950), a book on putative space travel by the physicist Alexander Ananoff, with whom Hergé began a correspondence in April 1950.
Background

According to literary critics Jean-Marc Lofficier and Randy Lofficier, possible fictional influences on Hergé's story include Jules Verne's 1870 novel Around the Moon and the 1950 American film Destination Moon.
Background
Hergé was certainly inspired by a number of photographic stills from the Destination Moon film which had been published.
Background
The computer system at the Sprodj space centre was visually based upon the UNIVAC I, the first computer to be created for non-military purposes.
Background
Hergé based his Moon rocket on the designs of the V-2 rocket which had been developed by Nazi scientists during World War II.
Background
The red-and-white checker pattern on Hergé's rocket was based upon an illustration of a V-2 which Hergé had come upon in Leslie Simon's 1947 book German Research in World War II.
Background
Hergé introduced into the story the character of Boris Jorgen, who had previously appeared as an antagonist in King Ottokar's Sceptre (1939).
Publication
On 7 September 1950, Hergé broke off the story with the statement "end of part one".
Publication
On 18 April 1951, he published an open letter in the magazine explaining his absence as a result of illness caused by exhaustion and included an illustration of himself sprawled out on an armchair.
Publication
Explorers on the Moon would resume after an eighteen-month hiatus, returning in the 9 April 1952 issue, accompanied with a summary of the story so far.
Republication
The story was collected together and published by Editions Casterman as On a Marché Sur La Lune in 1954.
Republication
Casterman were unhappy with this title, which translates as "We Walked on the Moon", but Hergé resolutely refused to make a change.
Critical analysis

Philippe Goddin praised the depiction of the rocket's landing as "a magnificent spectacle, well worth the double space spread given by Hergé", also highlighting what he perceived as the ending's "unprecedented dramatic tension".
Critical analysis

Apostolidès opined that despite being a "fussy and somewhat ridiculous character", through his scientific achievements Calculus grows to the "stature of a giant" in this arc, eclipsing Sir Francis Haddock (from The Secret of the Unicorn) as the series' "founding ancestor".
Critical analysis
He suggested that Explorers on the Moon was "perhaps both the most wildly adventurous and the most contemplative" instalment in the series.
Critical analysis

Commenting on the scene in which Haddock smuggles a whisky bottle inside the Guide to Astronomy, he states "the text, in this case, is hollow, smuggling something else", which he believed was a reversal of the appearance of a parchment hidden within a model ship in The Secret of the Unicorn.
Adaptation

In 1957, the animation company Belvision Studios produced a string of colour adaptations based on Hergé's original comics, adapting eight of the Adventures into a series of daily five-minute episodes.
Adaptation
In 1991, a second animated series based upon The Adventures of Tintin was produced, this time as a collaboration between the French studio Ellipse and the Canadian animation company Nelvana.

indy_scott_pilgrum_vol_1.title: Scott Pilgrim

caption: Scott Pilgrim, Vol. 1 coloured edition cover by Bryan Lee O'Malley and Nathan Fairbairn, featuring the titular character Scott Pilgrim

sents: lead
Scott Pilgrim is a series of graphic novels written and illustrated by Canadian author and comic book artist Bryan Lee O'Malley.
lead
The original edition of the series consists of six digest size black-and-white volumes, released between August 2004 and July 2010, by Portland-based independent comic book publisher Oni Press.
lead
It was later republished by Fourth Estate, an imprint of HarperCollins.
lead
Full-colour hardback volumes, coloured by Nathan Fairbairn, were released from August 2012 to May 2015.
lead

The series revolves around the titular Scott Pilgrim, a slacker and part-time musician who lives in Toronto and plays bass ‍in a rock band, as he dates a high school student after a traumatic breakup.
lead
He simultaneously starts a tentative romance with American delivery girl Ramona Flowers, soon discovering she has seven evil exes.
lead

They are manipulated into targeting Scott in combat by her most recent ex-boyfriend, Gideon Graves, forcing both Scott and Ramona to come to terms with their respective pasts, relationships, and behaviors.
lead
The Scott Pilgrim series received widespread acclaim from critics for its artwork, humor, themes, characters, influences, storyline and visual style, and it has garnered a significant cult following.
Publications
Scott Pilgrim Print Collection 2004-2024 was released September 24, 2024 and will contained 21 prints by Bryan Lee O'Malley including never-before-seen art.
Publications
A collector's box containing all six volumes and a fold-in poster was released in North America on November 3, 2010.
Publications
Scott Pilgrim's Precious Little Life was re-released in colour in August 2012, with the others being released on an irregular schedule, the last in May 2015.
Publications
The entire series was re-released in colour again in July 2019 as the Scott Pilgrim Color Collection, collected into 3 larger-format paperback volumes.
Development

O'Malley wanted to write a shōnen-style comic book series, although he had only read one such series at the time, Ranma ½; in the early 2000s, Japanese manga had not yet achieved significant popularity in North America.
Development
In 2002, O'Malley's roommate, who worked in a comic book store, brought the book to him while O'Malley was working on Lost at Sea and was planning Scott Pilgrim.
Development
O'Malley said that Osamu Tezuka began influencing his work as he created Volumes 3 and 4.
Development
When writing the series, O'Malley's first step was developing the direction of the story by creating notes in notebooks, sketchbooks, and computer text files.
Development
O'Malley himself created most of the Scott Pilgrim material.
Development
When production on Volume 6 had begun, O'Malley had hired two assistants.
Development
The backgrounds in Volume 6 are more detailed than the backgrounds in the previous volumes (O'Malley said that "[m]ost fans don't seem to notice the change").
Development
I like the term 'manga-influenced comics,' but I only like it because no one else likes it."
Development
O'Malley said that he expected Scott Pilgrim to sell around 1,000 copies.
Development
O'Malley said that the most difficult portion of Scott Pilgrim to write was the ending.
Development
O'Malley deliberately did not consider constructing the ending until he began writing Volume 5.
Development
He intended for Volumes 5 and 6 to reflect one single story, with 5 being the "darkest hour" and 6 being the "redemption arc".
Development

To illustrate his reasoning for eventually ending the Scott Pilgrim series, O'Malley used a quote from famed Belgian comics writer and artist Hergé, creator of the Adventures of Tintin comic book series, from 1929 until his death in 1983.
Development
The cover of the third Japanese Scott Pilgrim volume, which includes content from the original volumes 5 and 6, was based on an illustration from Street Fighter Alpha 2 (Street Fighter Zero 2).
Development
O'Malley used the font Swiss 721 Bold Condensed, which was also used in the film.
Development
M04 FATAL FURY is the pixel font used in Book 4 and beyond.
Synopsis

Scott is initially dating a 17-year-old high school student named Knives Chau, but he soon falls for a mysterious American woman named Ramona Flowers, who recently moved to Toronto and appeared in his dreams.
Main characters
Scott William Pilgrim - The titular protagonist, a 23-year-old slacker who is a bassist in the local garage band "Sex Bob-Omb" and cited as the best fighter in Ontario.
Main characters
Knives Chau - An innocent 17-year-old high school student of Chinese descent whom Scott is dating at the start of the series.
''Scott Pilgrim's Precious Little Life'' (Volume 1)
When Sex Bob-Omb begins to play anyway, a mysterious man crashes through the ceiling and attacks Scott, introducing himself as Matthew Patel, Ramona's first "Evil Ex-Boyfriend".
''Scott Pilgrim's Precious Little Life'' (Volume 1)
Scott defeats Matthew, shattering him into $2.10 in Canadian currency.
''Scott Pilgrim vs. the World'' (Volume 2)
On his next date with Ramona, she suggests he cut his hair, though he is averse to the idea, associating his last haircut with a previous breakup.
''Scott Pilgrim vs. the World'' (Volume 2)

Thinking quickly, Scott tricks Lucas into attempting a dangerous skateboard grind on the Casa Loma stairway rails; Lucas flies down the stairs at supersonic speeds and combusts at the bottom, leaving behind about $14 in coins and a mithril skateboard.
''Scott Pilgrim and the Infinite Sadness'' (Volume 3)
Envy proposes a challenge for Scott and Todd: a fight to the death at Honest Ed's—whoever reaches the end of the store first wins.
''Scott Pilgrim Gets It Together'' (Volume 4)
Knives and Kim accidentally out themselves as bisexual and make out while blackout drunk, with only Scott remembering it, and Stephen and Julie break up.
''Scott Pilgrim Gets It Together'' (Volume 4)
The destruction left behind causes Scott to get fired.
''Scott Pilgrim vs. the Universe'' (Volume 5)
With Gideon being the last evil ex to battle, Scott grows paranoid, perceiving anyone with glasses as Gideon.
''Scott Pilgrim's Finest Hour'' (Volume 6)
Jobless, kicked out of Sex Bob-Omb, and scared to face Gideon, Scott spends most of his time alone in his apartment playing video games.
''Scott Pilgrim's Finest Hour'' (Volume 6)
When he is finally convinced to go outside, he tries to reconnect with the now-18-year-old Knives, desiring casual sex, but Knives states that she has moved on.
''Scott Pilgrim's Finest Hour'' (Volume 6)
Ramona apologizes for leaving him but admits she has only returned to confront Gideon, not to restart their relationship.
''Scott Pilgrim's Finest Hour'' (Volume 6)
Scott uses his extra life from Part 3 to bring himself back to life, bringing Ramona with him.
''Scott Pilgrim's Finest Hour'' (Volume 6)
Gideon bursts into $7,777,777 worth of coins, pouring down painfully on the crowd.
''Scott Pilgrim's Finest Hour'' (Volume 6)
Scott and Kim start a new band called Shatter Band, but they only play covers and for fun.
Critical reception
Publishers Weekly ranked the third volume, Scott Pilgrim & The Infinite Sadness, as one of the best comic books of 2006 in a critics' poll.
Critical reception
Scott Pilgrim was ranked 85th on Wizard magazine's 2008 list of the "200 Greatest Comic Characters of All Time".
Critical reception
In 2011 Scott Pilgrim was ranked 69th in IGN's list of the top 100 comic book heroes.
Awards

In 2005, O'Malley won the Doug Wright Award for Best Emerging Talent for the first volume of Scott Pilgrim and was nominated for three Harvey Awards (Best New Talent, Best Cartoonist and Best Graphic Album of Original Work).
Awards
In 2006, O'Malley was awarded Outstanding Canadian Comic Book Cartoonist (Writer/Artist) in the Joe Shuster Awards.
Awards
O'Malley was nominated for a 2006 Eisner Award in the category Best Writer/Artist—Humor, for Scott Pilgrim Vs.
Awards
O'Malley and Scott Pilgrim were also nominated for two 2006 Eagle Awards, and nominated for a second Wright Award (for Scott Pilgrim Vs.
Awards
The series was also awarded a spot in Entertainment Weekly's 2007 A-List.
Awards
In 2010, O'Malley won his first Eisner Award in the "Best Humor Publication" category for Scott Pilgrim Vs.
Film
The film Scott Pilgrim vs. the World was released on August 13, 2010.
Film
The 2-disc edition includes soundtracks, animation (when Scott dates Kim), and a making-of.
''Scott Pilgrim vs. The Animation''
At the 2010 San Diego Comic-Con, Alison Pill (who plays Kim Pine in the movie), revealed that her character's past relationship with Scott will be explored in other media.
''Scott Pilgrim vs. The Animation''
One of them will be the Volume 2 high school stuff with Kim and Lisa Miller.
''Scott Pilgrim vs. The Animation''
I don't know how long it will be but the rough they showed me was like 5 minutes.
''Scott Pilgrim vs. The Animation''
The animated short, entitled Scott Pilgrim vs. the Animation, was produced by Titmouse, Inc. and aired on Adult Swim on August 12, 2010, later being released on their website.
Video games
The World, was announced during the 2009 San Diego Comic-Con and was developed by Ubisoft Montreal, released alongside the film.
Video games

The game is a four-player side-scroller influenced by 8-bit and 16-bit video games, with players able to play as Scott Pilgrim, Ramona Flowers, Kim Pine and Stephen Stills; players can also unlock NegaScott, while Knives Chau and Wallace Wells were added as playable characters via downloadable content.
Video games
The game was released on PlayStation Network on August 10, 2010 and Xbox Live Arcade on August 25, 2010.
Video games
On December 30, 2014, Scott Pilgrim vs. the World: The Game was delisted from the Xbox Live Arcade and PlayStation Network.
Video games

On September 10, 2020, to celebrate its 10th anniversary, Ubisoft announced that the game would finally be re-released with all downloadable content included as Scott Pilgrim vs. the World: The GameComplete Edition.
Video games
The game was released on PlayStation 4, Xbox One, Nintendo Switch, PC, and Stadia, on January 14, 2021.
Video games

On June 6, 2025, a new Scott Pilgrim game, titled Scott Pilgrim EX, was announced to be in development by Tribute Games, a studio founded by members of the Scott Pilgrim vs. the World: The Game development team, with Anamanaguchi returning to compose the soundtrack.
Video games
Scott and Ramona return as playable characters, now joined by Matthew Patel, Lucas Lee, Roxie Richter, Robot-01, and Gideon Graves.
Video games
The game was released on March 3, 2026.
Mobile comic
The app uses movement, sound and vibration to create an original reading experience and includes extra material hidden in the scenes of the comic.
Anime series
On March 30, 2023, it was announced that the original cast from the movie would reprise their roles for the television series, with Anamanaguchi providing original music.
Anime series
The series, titled Scott Pilgrim Takes Off, was released on November 17, 2023, and serves as both a continuation and alternate retelling of the books' events.

indy_strangers_in_paradice_1.title: Strangers in Paradise

caption: Pocket book #1 cover

sents: lead
Strangers in Paradise is a creator-owned comic book series, written and drawn by Terry Moore, which debuted in 1993.
lead

Principally the story of a love triangle between two women and one man, Strangers in Paradise began as a slice-of-life dramedy that later expanded to incorporate aspects of the crime and thriller genres.
lead
Moore has remained the sole creator throughout the run, with the exception of a superhero dream sequence drawn by Jim Lee that opens Volume 3, issue #1.
lead
The artwork was originally presented in Moore's distinctive black-and-white style, aside from two full colour dream sequences, which included the aforementioned superhero panels.
lead
The majority of the run has been published under Moore's creator-owned imprint, Abstract Studio.
lead
The first issue was published in November 1993, and the original series reached its planned conclusion in 2007 with issue #90 of Volume 3.
lead
In 2018, Moore officially revived the series as Strangers in Paradise XXV for the 25th anniversary.
Origins and publication history
Moore told Omar Valdivieso in a Near Mint Condition interview that he was inspired by girls' comics and Ian Fleming's James Bond novels.
Origins and publication history

SiP, as it is commonly known, began as a three-issue miniseries published by Antarctic Press in 1993, which focused entirely on the relationship between the three main characters and Francine's unfaithful boyfriend.
Origins and publication history
Thirteen issues were published under Moore's own "Abstract Studio" imprint, and these make up "Volume 2".
Origins and publication history
The series moved to Image Comics' Homage imprint for the start of "Volume 3", but after eight issues moved back to Abstract Studio, where it continued with the same numbering.
Origins and publication history
Volume 3 concluded at issue #90, released on June 6, 2007.
Origins and publication history
Moore revived the series as Strangers in Paradise XXV in 2018 for the 25th anniversary.
Plot
Francine considers Katchoo her best, oldest friend.
Plot
Katchoo makes no secret of her romantic attraction to Francine, creating tension each time Francine remains wary of fully committing to her.
Characters
Katchoo has been in love with her best friend, Francine, for most of her life, though she has complicated romantic feelings for her only male friend, David, as well.
Characters
Katchoo was ranked 69th in Comics Buyer's Guides "100 Sexiest Women in Comics" list.
Characters
Francine Helena Peters-Silver Katchoo's kind-hearted best friend, Francine struggles with her weight and her self-image, never quite able to see the beauty in herself that Katchoo is enamored with.
Characters
Francine was ranked 86th in Comics Buyer's Guide "100 Sexiest Women in Comics" list.
Characters
Though she employs only women and expresses a profound abhorrence of the male gender itself, Darcy harbors an intense, incestuous love for her brother David.
Characters
Mary Beth "Tambi" Baker A brutal enforcer loyal to Darcy Parker, Tambi is skilled in not only the deadly arts, but in business and strategy.
Characters
Griffin Silver An aging rock star admired by Katchoo in her youth, Griffin's songs were printed in the series long before the character made his first appearance.
Characters
Brad Silver A charming, handsome gynecologist, Brad at first appears to be an ideal husband for Francine, but their inability to communicate drives a wedge between them.
Awards
Strangers in Paradise received the Eisner Award for Best Serialized Story in 1996 for "I Dream of You" as well as the National Cartoonists Society's Reuben Award for Best Comic Book in 2003.
Awards
The series also won the GLAAD Media Award for Outstanding Comic Book in 2000 and 2008 and also nominated for the award in 2002, 2003, 2004, 2005, 2006 and 2019.
Awards
As such, Strangers in Paradise has the distinction of being the most-nominated comic in the history of the award.
Collected editions
Strangers in Paradise calendars: 1999, 2000, 2002, 2003, 2004.
Merchandise
Two limited edition statuettes of Katchoo were produced by Clayburn Moore as the first in a planned series of three statues based around the series.
Merchandise
In the first, she is standing in a skimpy black dress, and in the second she is reclining in a bath wearing her leather jacket and holding a drink and a gun.
Merchandise
In 2009, Shocker Toys released a Katchoo figure as part of the first series of its "Indie Spotlight" line.
Merchandise

In 1996, a series of trading cards was released by Comic Images, consisting of a 90-card base set plus extra collector's cards, such as the 500 'autograph cards' that featured Terry Moore's signature and information on the creation of SiP.
Merchandise
Also produced was a matching SiP binder, which came with 12 9-pocket sleeves to hold the cards.
Film adaptation
In Autumn of 2017, Angela Robinson and Moore announced a film adaptation of the comic.

indy_haet_1.title: Hate (comics)

title: Hate
caption: Cover art for Hate #1.
Art by Peter Bagge.

sents: lead
Hate is a comic book by writer-artist Peter Bagge.
lead
First published by Fantagraphics in 1990 it ran for 30 issues, and was one of the best-selling alternative comics of the 1990s, at its height selling 30,000 copies an issue.
lead
In 2000 Bagge revived the series in Hate Annual, a yearly comic that continues the story after Hate in short stories, and includes writings on libertarianism, culture, and topical cartoons.
lead
Hate follows the life of Buddy Bradley, in a continuation of events from Bagge's strip "The Bradleys" from former publications Neat Stuff.
lead
It is set for the first half in Seattle and later in suburban New Jersey.
lead

Buddy has to deal with the end of adolescence, reluctantly growing up, his relationships with a host of unpleasant acquaintances he has to class as friends, working in dead-end jobs and having no direction in life.
lead
Bagge used memories of events from his own life as material.
lead
Hate has been referenced by many commentators as an important example of Generation X comic culture and grunge culture in general.
Publication history
First published by Fantagraphics from 1990 to 1998, it ran for 30 issues, and was one of the best-selling alternative comics.
Publication history
The series continues in Hate Annual, (9) yearly collection of comics stories and articles that began in 2000.
Publication history
A major story and format change took place in issue #16, when Buddy moved from Seattle back home to New Jersey, at which point the comic, once in black-and-white, changed to color.
Publication history
With issue #16, Bagge also started using an inker (rather unusual for an alternative comic book), Jim Blanchard.
Publication history

Hate'''s final five issues were 48-page anthologies, featuring a main Buddy Bradley story and then a series of short backup stories by cartoonists such as Rick Altergott, Dame Darcy, and Kevin Scalzo.
Publication history
In February, 2024, Fantagraphics announced a new series by Bagge entitled Hate Revisited, which sees Buddy and his family dealing with modern time shenanigans.
Publication history
In March, 2026, Fantagraphcis published Butch #1: A Hate Comic'', a one-shot featuring Buddy Bradley's younger brother.
Supporting characters
Probably the most irresponsible, selfish and hopeless of all the characters.
Supporting characters
Valerie Russo, Buddy's first serious girlfriend, an upper middle class, apparently self-confident feminist with nymphomaniacal and manic depressive tendencies.
Supporting characters
Jay Spano, an old friend of Buddy's whom he met at a record store.
Cultural impact
In Hate #3, Bagge ran a competition to "Win a Date With Stinky", to which many fans submitted artwork and photographs.
Cultural impact
In issue #6, Bagge ran another contest, this time a "Buddy Bradley Look-Alike Contest," which hundreds entered.
In other media
Hate has been optioned as a movie or TV series numerous times, and in development as an animated series at MTV, HBO and Fox at various times since 1995.
In other media
A four-minute pilot for an animated Hate series was made in 1995, co-written by Bagge and Steve Loter, directed by Loter, and featuring music by Mudhoney.
Spain
A Spanish language edition of Hate, translated to Odio (which means "hatred") was published by Ediciones La Cúpula starting in 1995.
Spain

Serrano, Odio, taking into account population differences, was comparatively more successful in Spain than its USA counterpart (10,000 copies sold per issue in Spain compared to 30,000 copies per issue for the USA.).
Spain

Benet Román, writing for the 14th annual Barcelona International Comic Fair in 1996, commented that "Bagge... knows how to capture some of the spirit of our time, using that most universal, affordable and difficult to produce medium: humor."
Germany
In Germany, the first fifteen issues of Hate were translated for the German market and published by Carlsen Comics under the title Leck Mich!
Germany
(literal: "Lick me!," which possibly most closely translates to "kiss it!", as in "kiss my ass").
Germany
Later color editions of Hate were issued in 1998 by Jochen Enterprises under the title Krass/Kraß (a slang term, meaning "phat," "cool," or "rad" – its conventional meaning is "crass").
Collections
Buddy Does Jersey (Fantagraphics, 2007, ) – collects Hate #16-#30.
